stories.title: 📜 1 Chronicles 1
summaryBullets: Adam, Seth, Enosh, (1:1).
Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, (1:2).
Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, Noah. (1:3).
The sons of Noah: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. (1:4).
The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. (1:5).
The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. (1:6).
And the sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, the Kittites, and the Rodanites. (1:7).
The sons of Ham: Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan. (1:8).
The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabta, Raamah, and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan. (1:9).
Cush was the father of Nimrod, who began to be a mighty one on the earth. (1:10).
Mizraim was the father of the Ludites, the Anamites, the Lehabites, the Naphtuhites, (1:11).
the Pathrusites, the Casluhites (from whom the Philistines came), and the Caphtorites. (1:12).
And Canaan was the father of Sidon his firstborn, and of the Hittites, (1:13).
the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites, (1:14).
the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites, (1:15).
the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites. (1:16).
The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, and Aram. The sons of Aram: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Meshech. (1:17).
Arphaxad was the father of Shelah, and Shelah was the father of Eber. (1:18).
Two sons were born to Eber: One was named Peleg, because in his days the earth was divided, and his brother was named Joktan. (1:19).
And Joktan was the father of Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, (1:20).
Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, (1:21).
Obal, Abimael, Sheba, (1:22).
Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. All these were sons of Joktan. (1:23).
So from Shem came Arphaxad, Shelah, (1:24).
Eber, Peleg, Reu, (1:25).
Serug, Nahor, Terah, (1:26).
and Abram (that is, Abraham). (1:27).
The sons of Abraham were Isaac and Ishmael. (1:28).
These are their genealogies: Nebaioth the firstborn of Ishmael, then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam, (1:29).
Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadad, Tema, (1:30).
Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah. These were the sons of Ishmael. (1:31).
The sons born to Keturah, Abraham’s concubine: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. The sons of Jokshan: Sheba and Dedan. (1:32).
The sons of Midian: Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All of these were Keturah’s sons. (1:33).
Abraham was the father of Isaac. The sons of Isaac: Esau and Israel. (1:34).
The sons of Esau: Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. (1:35).
The sons of Eliphaz: Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, and Kenaz; and by Timna, Amalek. (1:36).
The sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. (1:37).
The sons of Seir: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan. (1:38).
The sons of Lotan: Hori and Homam. Timna was Lotan’s sister. (1:39).
The sons of Shobal: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam. The sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah. (1:40).
The son of Anah: Dishon. The sons of Dishon: Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran. (1:41).
The sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan. The sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran. (1:42).
These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the Israelites: Bela son of Beor. His city was named Dinhabah. (1:43).
When Bela died, Jobab son of Zerah from Bozrah reigned in his place. (1:44).
When Jobab died, Husham from the land of the Temanites reigned in his place. (1:45).
When Husham died, Hadad son of Bedad, who defeated Midian in the country of Moab, reigned in his place. And the name of his city was Avith. (1:46).
When Hadad died, Samlah from Masrekah reigned in his place. (1:47).
When Samlah died, Shaul from Rehoboth on the Euphrates reigned in his place. (1:48).
When Shaul died, Baal-hanan son of Achbor reigned in his place. (1:49).
When Baal-hanan died, Hadad reigned in his place. His city was named Pau, and his wife’s name was Mehetabel daughter of Matred, the daughter of Me-zahab. (1:50).
Then Hadad died. Now the chiefs of Edom were Timna, Alvah, Jetheth, (1:51).
Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon, (1:52).
Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar, (1:53).
Magdiel, and Iram. These were the chiefs of Edom. (1:54).
crossRefs: Genesis 5:1-32: The line from Adam through Seth to Noah and his three sons, with each man's years.
Genesis 10:1-32: The nations that spread out from Shem, Ham, and Japheth after the flood.
Genesis 11:10-26: The line from Shem down to Terah, the father of Abram.
Genesis 25:12-18: The twelve sons of Ishmael, named with the settlements they held.
Genesis 36:1-43: Esau's sons, the chiefs of Edom, and the kings who reigned before Israel had a king.

translationNotes.note: A family list was a legal document, not a family memento. Land stayed with the clan that received it, and a claim to a field rested on proving descent (Numbers 27:1-11, 36:6-9). Priesthood ran the same way: at the return from Babylon, priests who could not find their entry in the register were struck off as unclean and barred from the altar (Ezra 2:61-63, Nehemiah 7:63-65). The throne ran the same way too, which is why the list in chapter 3 keeps going past the exile.

The word means generations or descendants, and it is the marker that divides the book of Genesis into sections (Genesis 5:1, 10:1, 11:10, 25:12, 36:1). Chronicles opens by running those same Genesis lists together with almost no verbs at all, and uses the word itself at verse 29 for Ishmael's sons. Nine chapters of names come before the narrative starts.

Verse 19 says one son was named Peleg 'because in his days the earth was divided.' The name is built from the verb palag, to split or divide, so the sentence explains itself in Hebrew and loses the connection in English. Genesis 10:25 records the same naming in the same words.

The nation descended from Esau, southeast of the Dead Sea in the red sandstone highlands of Seir. The name plays on the red stew Esau sold his birthright for (Genesis 25:30) and on his own red colouring (Genesis 25:25). Edom refused Israel passage on the way out of Egypt (Numbers 20:14-21), and the grudge runs through the prophets to Obadiah's whole book.

Verses 43-51 list eight men who ruled Edom in succession before any king reigned in Israel. None is the son of the man before him, so this was not a dynasty passed down a family but rule that moved from town to town. Edom had settled kingship while Israel still had none.

stories.keyTakeaway: Adam's line extends through Noah and his sons, with genealogies traced through Shem to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; the chapter also lists descendants of Ishmael and Esau, and records the kings and chiefs who ruled in Edom before any Israelite king reigned.

stories.title: 📜 1 Chronicles 2
summaryBullets: These were the sons of Israel: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, (2:1).
Dan, Joseph, Benjamin, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher. (2:2).
The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, and Shelah. These three were born to him by Bath-shua the Canaanite. Er, Judah’s firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the LORD. So the LORD put him to death. (2:3).
Tamar, Judah’s daughter-in-law, bore to him Perez and Zerah. Judah had five sons in all. (2:4).
The sons of Perez: Hezron and Hamul. (2:5).
The sons of Zerah: Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Dara— five in all. (2:6).
The son of Carmi: Achar, who brought trouble upon Israel by violating the ban on devoted things. (2:7).
The son of Ethan: Azariah. (2:8).
The sons who were born to Hezron: Jerahmeel, Ram, and Caleb. (2:9).
Ram was the father of Amminadab, and Amminadab was the father of Nahshon, a leader of the descendants of Judah. (2:10).
Nahshon was the father of Salmon, and Salmon was the father of Boaz. (2:11).
Boaz was the father of Obed, and Obed was the father of Jesse. (2:12).
Jesse was the father of Eliab his firstborn; Abinadab was born second, Shimea third, (2:13).
Nethanel fourth, Raddai fifth, (2:14).
Ozem sixth, and David seventh. (2:15).
Their sisters were Zeruiah and Abigail. And the three sons of Zeruiah were Abishai, Joab, and Asahel. (2:16).
Abigail was the mother of Amasa, whose father was Jether the Ishmaelite. (2:17).
Caleb son of Hezron had children by his wife Azubah and by Jerioth. These were the sons of Azubah: Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon. (2:18).
When Azubah died, Caleb married Ephrath, who bore to him Hur. (2:19).
Hur was the father of Uri, and Uri was the father of Bezalel. (2:20).
Later, Hezron slept with the daughter of Machir the father of Gilead. He had married her when he was sixty years old, and she bore to him Segub. (2:21).
Segub was the father of Jair, who had twenty-three cities in the land of Gilead. (2:22).
But Geshur and Aram captured Havvoth-jair, along with Kenath and its sixty surrounding villages. All these were descendants of Machir the father of Gilead. (2:23).
After Hezron died in Caleb-ephrathah, his wife Abijah bore to him Ashhur the father of Tekoa. (2:24).
The sons of Jerahmeel the firstborn of Hezron: Ram his firstborn, Bunah, Oren, Ozem, and Ahijah. (2:25).
Jerahmeel had another wife named Atarah, who was the mother of Onam. (2:26).
The sons of Ram the firstborn of Jerahmeel: Maaz, Jamin, and Eker. (2:27).
The sons of Onam: Shammai and Jada. The sons of Shammai: Nadab and Abishur. (2:28).
Abishur’s wife was named Abihail, and she bore to him Ahban and Molid. (2:29).
The sons of Nadab: Seled and Appaim. Seled died without children. (2:30).
The son of Appaim: Ishi. The son of Ishi: Sheshan. The son of Sheshan: Ahlai. (2:31).
The sons of Jada the brother of Shammai: Jether and Jonathan. Jether died without children. (2:32).
The sons of Jonathan: Peleth and Zaza. These were the descendants of Jerahmeel. (2:33).
Sheshan had no sons, but only daughters. He also had an Egyptian servant named Jarha. (2:34).
Sheshan gave his daughter in marriage to his servant Jarha, and she bore to him Attai. (2:35).
Attai was the father of Nathan, Nathan was the father of Zabad, (2:36).
Zabad was the father of Ephlal, Ephlal was the father of Obed, (2:37).
Obed was the father of Jehu, Jehu was the father of Azariah, (2:38).
Azariah was the father of Helez, Helez was the father of Elasah, (2:39).
Elasah was the father of Sismai, Sismai was the father of Shallum, (2:40).
Shallum was the father of Jekamiah, and Jekamiah was the father of Elishama. (2:41).
The sons of Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel: Mesha his firstborn, who was the father of Ziph, and Mareshah his second son, who was the father of Hebron. (2:42).
The sons of Hebron: Korah, Tappuah, Rekem, and Shema. (2:43).
Shema was the father of Raham the father of Jorkeam, and Rekem was the father of Shammai. (2:44).
The son of Shammai was Maon, and Maon was the father of Beth-zur. (2:45).
Caleb’s concubine Ephah was the mother of Haran, Moza, and Gazez. Haran was the father of Gazez. (2:46).
The sons of Jahdai: Regem, Jotham, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah, and Shaaph. (2:47).
Caleb’s concubine Maacah was the mother of Sheber and Tirhanah. (2:48).
She was also the mother of Shaaph father of Madmannah, and of Sheva father of Machbenah and Gibea. Caleb’s daughter was Acsah. (2:49).
These were the descendants of Caleb. The sons of Hur the firstborn of Ephrathah: Shobal the father of Kiriath-jearim, (2:50).
Salma the father of Bethlehem, and Hareph the father of Beth-gader. (2:51).
These were the descendants of Shobal the father of Kiriath-jearim: Haroeh, half the Manahathites, (2:52).
and the clans of Kiriath-jearim— the Ithrites, Puthites, Shumathites, and Mishraites. From these descended the Zorathites and Eshtaolites. (2:53).
The descendants of Salma: Bethlehem, the Netophathites, Atroth-beth-joab, half the Manahathites, the Zorites, (2:54).
and the clans of the scribes who lived at Jabez— the Tirathites, Shimeathites, and Sucathites. These are the Kenites who came from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab. (2:55).
crossRefs: Genesis 46:8-27: The seventy sons of Israel who went down into Egypt, listed by mother.
Genesis 38:1-30: Judah, Tamar, and the birth of the twins Perez and Zerah.
Ruth 4:18-22: The ten generations from Perez to David, closing the book of Ruth.
Joshua 7:16-26: Achan of Zerah's line is taken by lot for the devoted things and stoned in the Valley of Achor.
Joshua 15:13-19: Caleb takes Hebron, and his daughter Achsah asks him for the upper and lower springs.

translationNotes.note: Verse 7 calls Achan 'the troubler of Israel, who was unfaithful in the matter of the devoted thing.' Herem meant a person or object handed over to God entirely and so removed from ordinary use, either destroyed or given to the sanctuary. Jericho was placed under herem in Joshua 6:17-19, which is why keeping a robe and silver from it cost Achan his life.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָכָר (Achar) - עָכַן (Achan) - עָכַר (akar), to trouble
translationNotes.note: Joshua 7 calls the man Achan. Chronicles spells the name Achar, which is the verb akar, to bring trouble on someone. Joshua 7:25 makes the same play out loud, 'Why have you troubled us? The LORD will trouble you today,' and names the place the Valley of Achor, the valley of trouble.

Verses 42 to 55 call men the father of Ziph, of Hebron, of Bethlehem, of Kiriath-jearim. In these lists av marks the founder of a settlement or the head of the clan that held it, not a man who begot a town. Read that way the section is a map of who owned what in Judah, which is what a land claim needed.

Verse 4 has Judah's daughter-in-law Tamar bearing him Perez and Zerah, which is the account in Genesis 38. Under levirate law a dead man's brother married the widow so the first son would carry the dead man's name and hold his land (Deuteronomy 25:5-10). Judah withheld his third son from Tamar, and the line to David in verses 10-15 runs through Perez, whom the elders name in the blessing at Ruth 4:12.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּצַלְאֵל (Betsalel), in the shadow of God
translationNotes.note: Verse 20 gives Hur, then Uri, then Bezalel. That is the craftsman of Exodus 31:1-11, filled with the Spirit of God for skill in gold, silver, bronze, stonecutting, and woodwork, who built the tabernacle and its furniture. He is the first person in Scripture said to be filled with the Spirit of God, and it is for a trade.

Verses 34-35 say Sheshan had no sons, only daughters, and gave a daughter in marriage to his Egyptian slave Jarha. With no son the property and the family name died, so a household married a daughter to a dependent who would raise sons inside the family rather than take them into another clan. The line that follows runs thirteen more generations, all of it counted as Jerahmeel's.

stories.keyTakeaway: The chapter lists the sons of Israel and traces genealogies from Judah through David, and from Hezron through his descendants Caleb and Jerahmeel, recording family lines and the towns their descendants inhabited.

stories.title: 📜 1 Chronicles 3
summaryBullets: These were the sons of David who were born to him in Hebron: The firstborn was Amnon by Ahinoam of Jezreel; the second was Daniel by Abigail of Carmel; (3:1).
the third was Absalom the son of Maacah daughter of King Talmai of Geshur; the fourth was Adonijah the son of Haggith; (3:2).
the fifth was Shephatiah by Abital; and the sixth was Ithream by his wife Eglah. (3:3).
These six sons were born to David in Hebron, where he reigned seven years and six months. And David reigned in Jerusalem thirty-three years, (3:4).
and these sons were born to him in Jerusalem: Shimea, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon. These four were born to him by Bathsheba daughter of Ammiel. (3:5).
David’s other sons were Ibhar, Elishua, Eliphelet, (3:6).
Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia, (3:7).
Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet— nine in all. (3:8).
These were all the sons of David, besides the sons by his concubines. And Tamar was their sister. (3:9).
Solomon’s son was Rehoboam: Abijah was his son, Asa his son, Jehoshaphat his son, (3:10).
Joram his son, Ahaziah his son, Joash his son, (3:11).
Amaziah his son, Azariah his son, Jotham his son, (3:12).
Ahaz his son, Hezekiah his son, Manasseh his son, (3:13).
Amon his son, and Josiah his son. (3:14).
The sons of Josiah: Johanan was the firstborn, Jehoiakim the second, Zedekiah the third, and Shallum the fourth. (3:15).
The successors of Jehoiakim: Jeconiah his son, and Zedekiah. (3:16).
The descendants of Jeconiah the captive: Shealtiel his son, (3:17).
Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazzar, Jekamiah, Hoshama, and Nedabiah. (3:18).
The sons of Pedaiah: Zerubbabel and Shimei. The children of Zerubbabel: Meshullam and Hananiah, their sister Shelomith, (3:19).
and five others: Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah, and Jushab-hesed. (3:20).
The descendants of Hananiah: Pelatiah, Jeshaiah, and the sons of Rephaiah, of Arnan, of Obadiah, and of Shecaniah. (3:21).
The six descendants of Shecaniah were Shemaiah and his sons: Hattush, Igal, Bariah, Neariah, and Shaphat. (3:22).
The sons of Neariah: Elioenai, Hizkiah, and Azrikam— three in all. (3:23).
The sons of Elioenai: Hodaviah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Delaiah, and Anani— seven in all. (3:24).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 3:2-5: The six sons born to David in Hebron, each listed with his mother.
2 Samuel 5:13-16: The sons born to David in Jerusalem after he took the city.
2 Kings 24:8-17: Jehoiachin surrenders to Babylon and is carried off with the treasures and the leading men.
Matthew 1:12-16: The line from Jeconiah through Shealtiel and Zerubbabel down to Joseph.
Haggai 2:20-23: Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel is told he will be made like a signet ring.

translationNotes.note: Verse 1 names David's second son, born to Abigail of Carmel, as Daniel. The parallel list at 2 Samuel 3:3 names the same son Chileab. Both readings stand in the text, and neither passage explains the difference. He is never mentioned again in either book.

Verse 5 calls Solomon's mother Bath-shua daughter of Ammiel. 2 Samuel 11:3 calls her Bathsheba daughter of Eliam. Ammiel and Eliam are the same two elements, am and el, in reverse order, and Chronicles regularly carries name forms that differ from Samuel and Kings.

Verse 15 lists Josiah's fourth son as Shallum. 2 Kings 23:30-34 has the people make Jehoahaz son of Josiah king, and Pharaoh Neco depose him after three months. Jeremiah 22:11 joins the two names outright, 'Shallum the son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned in place of Josiah his father.'

One king carries three names in Scripture: Jehoiachin (2 Kings 24:8), Jeconiah (verse 16 here), and Coniah (Jeremiah 22:24). All three are the same man, taken to Babylon in 597 BC at eighteen. Babylonian ration tablets excavated at Babylon list 'Yaukin king of the land of Yahudu' and his sons drawing oil from the royal stores, which matches 2 Kings 25:27-30.

Verse 19 lists Zerubbabel among the sons of Pedaiah. Ezra 3:2, Haggai 1:1, and Matthew 1:12 all call him the son of Shealtiel, Pedaiah's older brother in verse 17. Both readings stand in the text. His name means seed of, or sown in, Babylon, and he was born in the exile and led the first return.

stories.keyTakeaway: David's sons born in Hebron and Jerusalem are listed, including Amnon, Daniel, Absalom, Adonijah, Shephatiah, Ithream, and later Solomon, Nathan, Shammua, and Shobab. The chapter then traces Solomon's line of descendants through the kings of Judah and into the post-exile period, ending with the sons of Elioenai.

headings.text: The Royal Line After the Exile

stories.title: 📜 1 Chronicles 4
summaryBullets: The descendants of Judah: Perez, Hezron, Carmi, Hur, and Shobal. (4:1).
Reaiah son of Shobal was the father of Jahath, and Jahath was the father of Ahumai and Lahad. These were the clans of the Zorathites. (4:2).
These were the sons of Etam: Jezreel, Ishma, and Idbash. And their sister was named Hazzelelponi. (4:3).
Penuel was the father of Gedor, and Ezer was the father of Hushah. These were the descendants of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah and the father of Bethlehem. (4:4).
Ashhur the father of Tekoa had two wives, Helah and Naarah. (4:5).
Naarah bore to him Ahuzzam, Hepher, Temeni, and Haahashtari. These were the descendants of Naarah. (4:6).
The sons of Helah were Zereth, Zohar, Ethnan, (4:7).
and Koz, who was the father of Anub and Zobebah and of the clans of Aharhel son of Harum. (4:8).
Now Jabez was more honorable than his brothers. His mother had named him Jabez, saying, “Because I bore him in pain.” (4:9).

And Jabez called out to the God of Israel, “If only You would bless me and enlarge my territory! May Your hand be with me and keep me from harm, so that I will be free from pain.” And God granted the request of Jabez. (4:10).
Chelub the brother of Shuhah was the father of Mehir, who was the father of Eshton. (4:11).
Eshton was the father of Beth-rapha, of Paseah, and of Tehinnah the father of Ir-nahash. These were the men of Recah. (4:12).
The sons of Kenaz: Othniel and Seraiah. The sons of Othniel: Hathath and Meonothai. (4:13).
Meonothai was the father of Ophrah, and Seraiah was the father of Joab, the father of those living in Ge-harashim, which was given this name because its people were craftsmen. (4:14).
The sons of Caleb son of Jephunneh: Iru, Elah, and Naam. The son of Elah: Kenaz. (4:15).
The sons of Jehallelel: Ziph, Ziphah, Tiria, and Asarel. (4:16).
The sons of Ezrah: Jether, Mered, Epher, and Jalon. And Mered’s wife Bithiah gave birth to Miriam, Shammai, and Ishbah the father of Eshtemoa. (4:17).

These were the children of Pharaoh’s daughter Bithiah. Mered also took a Judean wife, who gave birth to Jered the father of Gedor, Heber the father of Soco, and Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah. (4:18).
The sons of Hodiah’s wife, the sister of Naham, were the fathers of Keilah the Garmite and of Eshtemoa the Maacathite. (4:19).
The sons of Shimon: Amnon, Rinnah, Ben-hanan, and Tilon. The descendants of Ishi: Zoheth and Ben-zoheth. (4:20).
The sons of Shelah son of Judah: Er the father of Lecah, Laadah the father of Mareshah and the clans of the linen workers at Beth-ashbea, (4:21).
Jokim, the men of Cozeba, and Joash and Saraph, who ruled in Moab and Jashubi-lehem. (These names are from ancient records.) (4:22).
These were the potters who lived at Netaim and Gederah. They lived there in the service of the king. (4:23).
The descendants of Simeon: Nemuel, Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, and Shaul. (4:24).
The sons of Shaul: Shallum, Mibsam, and Mishma. (4:25).
The sons of Mishma: Hammuel, Zaccur, and Shimei. (4:26).
Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters, but his brothers did not have many children, so their whole clan did not become as numerous as the sons of Judah. (4:27).
They lived in Beersheba, Moladah, Hazar-shual, (4:28).
Bilhah, Ezem, Tolad, (4:29).
Bethuel, Hormah, Ziklag, (4:30).
Beth-marcaboth, Hazar-susim, Beth-biri, and Shaaraim. These were their cities until the reign of David. (4:31).
And their villages were Etam, Ain, Rimmon, Tochen, and Ashan— five towns— (4:32).
and all their surrounding villages as far as Baal. These were their settlements, and they kept a genealogical record: (4:33).
Meshobab, Jamlech, Joshah son of Amaziah, (4:34).
Joel, Jehu son of Joshibiah (son of Seraiah, son of Asiel), (4:35).
Elioenai, Jaakobah, Jeshohaiah, Asaiah, Adiel, Jesimiel, Benaiah, (4:36).
and Ziza son of Shiphi (son of Allon, son of Jedaiah, son of Shimri, son of Shemaiah). (4:37).
These men listed by name were the leaders of their clans. Their families increased greatly, (4:38).
and they journeyed to the entrance of Gedor, to the east side of the valley, in search of pasture for their flocks. (4:39).
There they found rich, good pasture, and the land was spacious, peaceful, and quiet; for some Hamites had lived there formerly. (4:40).

These who were noted by name came in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah. They attacked the Hamites in their dwellings as well as the Meunites who were there, devoting them to destruction even to this day. Then they settled in their place, because there was pasture for their flocks. (4:41).
And five hundred of these Simeonites led by Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi, went to Mount Seir (4:42).
and struck down the remnant of the Amalekites who had escaped. And they have lived there to this day. (4:43).
crossRefs: Joshua 19:1-9: Simeon's inheritance is carved out inside Judah's territory because Judah's share was too large.
Genesis 49:5-7: Jacob says Simeon and Levi will be divided in Jacob and scattered in Israel.
Exodus 17:8-16: Amalek attacks Israel at Rephidim and the LORD swears to blot out Amalek's memory.
1 Samuel 15:1-9: Saul is sent to destroy Amalek and spares Agag and the best of the livestock.
Numbers 26:12-14: The Simeonite clans counted in Moab, down to 22,200 from 59,300 a generation earlier.

translationNotes.note: Verse 9 says his mother named him Jabez 'because I bore him in pain.' The name is the word for pain with two of its letters swapped, so the Hebrew hears the wordplay and the English cannot. His request in verse 10 to 'enlarge my territory' asks for gevul, the boundary line of a family's land, the thing every name in these chapters exists to secure.

Verses 17-18 record an Egyptian princess married into the tribe of Judah. Her name is built from bat, daughter, and Yah, the short form of the covenant name of God, so a daughter of Pharaoh is on record carrying the name of the God of Israel. The text says nothing more about how the marriage came about.

Verse 21 names clans of linen workers at Beth-ashbea and verse 23 potters at Netaim and Gederah who 'lived there in the service of the king.' These are hereditary trade guilds working on the crown's account, paid in land and rations rather than wages. Excavation across Judah has turned up more than two thousand jar handles stamped lmlk, 'belonging to the king,' the output of exactly this kind of royal workshop.

The towns listed in verses 28-32, Beersheba, Moladah, Hormah, Ziklag, sit inside Judah's territory, because Simeon never received a separate block of land. Joshua 19:1-9 says Simeon's inheritance lay in the middle of Judah's, since Judah's portion was too large for it. Verse 27 records the tribe staying small, and by the monarchy it is absorbed.

A raiding people of the Negev and Sinai, descended from Esau's grandson (Genesis 36:12). They struck Israel's stragglers at the rear coming out of Egypt (Deuteronomy 25:17-18), which is why the war with them never closes. Verse 43 records Simeonites wiping out the last Amalekite survivors at Seir, generations after Saul failed to.

stories.keyTakeaway: Genealogies of Judah and Simeon are recorded, including Jabez, who prayed to God for blessing and protection and received his request. Later, during Hezekiah's reign, Simeonite leaders and their clans expanded eastward, destroying Hamites and Meunites and settling their land, while others invaded Seir and killed the remaining Amalekites.

translationNotes.note: Verses 1-2 say Reuben's birthright passed to Joseph's sons because he defiled his father's bed (Genesis 35:22, 49:3-4). The bekorah was a double share of the inheritance, twice what any other son got (Deuteronomy 21:17). Joseph collects it literally: Ephraim and Manasseh are each counted as a full tribe with its own land (Genesis 48:5), so his line takes two portions.

A tent-dwelling people east of Gilead, fought in verses 10 and 19-22 alongside Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab. Jetur and Naphish are named among Ishmael's twelve sons at Genesis 25:15. The plunder taken in verse 21, fifty thousand camels and a quarter of a million sheep, is herd wealth rather than city wealth, which is what these peoples held.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֲרֹעֵר (Aroer) - נְבוֹ (Nevo) - בַּעַל מְעוֹן (Baal Meon)
translationNotes.note: The Reubenite towns of verse 8 sit on the tableland east of the Dead Sea, contested ground between Israel and Moab. All three are named on the Mesha Stele, a black basalt monument set up by Mesha king of Moab around 840 BC and found at Dhiban in 1868, which records Moab retaking Nebo and Baal-meon and rebuilding Aroer, and names the men of Gad as the previous occupants.

The empire on the upper Tigris, centred on Nineveh, Calah, and Ashur, that dominated the Near East from about 900 to 612 BC. Its standard policy after conquest was mass deportation: move the leading families out, settle foreigners in, and break the nation's ability to regroup. Verse 26 records the first stage of that policy falling on Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, resettled at Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river Gozan.

Verse 26 names 'Pul king of Assyria, that is, Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria,' treating the two as one man. Assyrian and Babylonian records agree: Babylonian King List A gives Pulu as the name under which Tiglath-pileser III held the throne of Babylon from 729 to 727 BC. He reigned in Assyria from 745 to 727 BC.

stories.keyTakeaway: Genealogies list the descendants of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, including their settlements and military strength; these tribes defeated the Hagrites with God's help but later turned to idolatry and were taken into exile by the king of Assyria.

translationNotes.note: Two different offices, and the chapter turns on the difference. Only Aaron's direct male line served as priests, and verse 49 limits them to the altar of burnt offering, the altar of incense, and the Most Holy Place. Every other family of Levi did the rest of the work of the sanctuary (verse 48) and could not offer sacrifice. Eligibility for either was proved by the descent recorded here.

Verses 50-53 run the succession from Aaron through Eleazar and Phinehas down to Zadok, the priest who anointed Solomon, and his son Ahimaaz. Verse 15 closes the same line by noting Jehozadak went into exile when Nebuchadnezzar carried Judah away. His son Jeshua is the high priest who comes back with Zerubbabel (Ezra 3:2), so the chain is unbroken across the exile.

Verses 31-47 set three Levites over the music, one from each of Levi's clans: Heman the Kohathite in the centre, Asaph the Gershonite at his right hand, Ethan the Merarite on his left. Verse 32 says they sang before the tent until Solomon built the house. Twelve psalms carry Asaph's name in their titles, Psalm 50 and Psalm 73 through 83; Psalm 88 is titled for Heman the Ezrahite and Psalm 89 for Ethan the Ezrahite.

Verses 57 and 67 hand Hebron and Shechem to the Levites as cities of refuge. Six towns, three each side of the Jordan, were set apart so a man who killed without intending to could outrun the blood-avenger, the go'el ha-dam, and stand trial before the assembly instead of being cut down on the road (Numbers 35:9-28, Joshua 20:1-9). He stayed there until the death of the high priest, then went home free.

Levi received no tribal block of land (Joshua 13:14). Instead the tribe got forty-eight towns scattered through the other tribes, each with pastureland reaching a thousand cubits, about 1,500 feet, out from the wall (Numbers 35:4-5). The effect was that priests and Levites lived inside every tribe rather than in one region.

stories.keyTakeaway: Genealogies trace the sons of Levi and their descendants, including the priestly line from Aaron through Phinehas and the musicians Heman, Asaph, and Ethan appointed by David; the chapter then details the towns and pasturelands distributed to the Kohathites, Gershonites, and Merarites throughout Israel's tribes.

translationNotes.note: The phrase running through this chapter is a muster term, not a compliment. Hayil covers strength, capability, and property together, so a gibbor hayil is a man of standing who could equip himself and turn out for war. Israel counted such men from twenty years old and upward (Numbers 1:3), which is why the totals here, 87,000 for Issachar and 26,000 for Asher, are draft rolls kept by family.

Verse 15 notes in passing that Zelophehad 'had only daughters.' That fact produced the inheritance ruling of Numbers 27:1-11, where his five daughters petition Moses and the land passes to them rather than out of the family. Numbers 36:6-9 then requires them to marry inside their father's tribe so the territory does not transfer to another tribe, and Joshua 17:3-6 records them receiving it.

Verses 21-23 tell of Ephraim's sons killed raiding cattle at Gath, and the son born afterward is named Beriah 'because tragedy had come upon his house.' The name and the phrase for misfortune are the same sounds in Hebrew. English keeps the name and drops the reason for it.

Verse 24 credits Sheerah, a woman, with building Lower and Upper Beth-horon. The two towns sit about ten miles northwest of Jerusalem and guard the Beth-horon pass, the main climb from the coastal plain and the Aijalon Valley up to the central ridge. Whoever held it controlled the road to Jerusalem, which is why armies keep fighting over it from Joshua 10:10-11 onward.

Verse 29 lists four towns along Manasseh's border, and all four are named at Joshua 17:11-13 and Judges 1:27 as towns the tribe could not drive the Canaanites out of. Megiddo guards the narrow pass through the Carmel ridge onto the Jezreel plain, the road every army between Egypt and Mesopotamia had to use. Beth-shean is where the Philistines fastened Saul's body to the wall (1 Samuel 31:10).

stories.keyTakeaway: Genealogical records list the descendants of Issachar, Benjamin, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Asher, including their family heads and fighting men; Ephraim's sons Ezer and Elead were killed by men of Gath when seizing livestock, and his daughter Sheerah built fortified cities.

and Abdon was his firstborn son, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Nadab, (8:30).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית אָב (bet av), father's house
translationNotes.note: The phrase repeated through this chapter names the working unit of Israelite society: an extended household of several generations under one senior man, holding one block of land. Tribe, then clan, then father's house, then the individual is the order Joshua 7:16-18 uses to search out Achan. A man's rights and obligations came through that unit, which is why the lists record heads of houses and where they lived.

Verse 8 says Shaharaim had sons in Moab 'after he had divorced his wives.' The Hebrew is simply that he sent them away. Deuteronomy 24:1-4 regulates the practice rather than creating it: the man writes her a certificate of divorce, a sefer keritut, puts it in her hand and sends her out, and he may never take her back once she has married another.

Verse 12 credits Shemed with building the two towns. They sit together on the coastal plain about eleven miles southeast of modern Tel Aviv, at the edge of Benjamin's reach toward the sea. Their men come back from Babylon as a named group (Ezra 2:33), the plain of Ono is where Sanballat tries to lure Nehemiah into a meeting (Nehemiah 6:2), and Lod is the Lydda where Peter heals Aeneas (Acts 9:32-35).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בִּנְיָמִין (Binyamin), son of the right hand
translationNotes.note: Verse 40 ends the chapter with Ulam's sons, 'mighty men of valor, archers.' Benjamin was known for missile troops: Judges 20:16 counts seven hundred left-handed men who could sling a stone at a hair and not miss, and 1 Chronicles 12:2 describes Benjaminites shooting arrows and slinging stones with either hand. The tribe whose name means son of the right hand kept producing left-handed fighters, Ehud among them (Judges 3:15).

Verses 33-34 call Saul's son Esh-baal and Jonathan's son Merib-baal. Samuel calls the same two men Ish-bosheth (2 Samuel 2:8) and Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 4:4). The element baal simply meant lord or master and was once used freely, but after Baal worship took hold the shameful word boshet was substituted in the names.

stories.keyTakeaway: The chapter traces the genealogy of Benjamin's descendants, listing the family lines of various chiefs who lived in Geba, Manahath, Aijalon, and Jerusalem; it includes the line from Ner to Saul and his sons, and ends with Azel's sons and the descendants of Ulam.

stories.title: 📜 1 Chronicles 9
summaryBullets: So all Israel was recorded in the genealogies written in the Book of the Kings of Israel. But Judah was exiled to Babylon because of their unfaithfulness. (9:1).
Now the first to resettle their own property in their cities were Israelites, priests, Levites, and temple servants. (9:2).
Some of the descendants of Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh lived in Jerusalem: (9:3).
Uthai son of Ammihud, the son of Omri, the son of Imri, the son of Bani, a descendant of Perez son of Judah. (9:4).
From the Shilonites: Asaiah the firstborn and his sons. (9:5).
From the Zerahites: Jeuel and 690 relatives. (9:6).
From the Benjamites: Sallu son of Meshullam, the son of Hodaviah, the son of Hassenuah; (9:7).
Ibneiah son of Jeroham; Elah son of Uzzi, the son of Michri; Meshullam son of Shephatiah, the son of Reuel, the son of Ibnijah; (9:8).
and 956 of their relatives according to their genealogy. All these men were heads of their families. (9:9).
From the priests: Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, and Jachin; (9:10).
Azariah son of Hilkiah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Zadok, the son of Meraioth, the son of Ahitub, the chief official of God’s temple; (9:11).
Adaiah son of Jeroham, the son of Pashhur, the son of Malchijah; Maasai son of Adiel, the son of Jahzerah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Meshillemith, the son of Immer; (9:12).
and 1,760 of their relatives, the heads of their families, able men for the work of the service of the house of God. (9:13).

Bakbakkar, Heresh, Galal, and Mattaniah son of Mica, the son of Zichri, the son of Asaph; (9:15).
Obadiah son of Shemaiah, the son of Galal, the son of Jeduthun; and Berechiah son of Asa, the son of Elkanah, who lived in the villages of the Netophathites. (9:16).
These were the gatekeepers: Shallum, Akkub, Talmon, Ahiman, and their relatives. Shallum was their chief; (9:17).
he was previously stationed at the King’s Gate on the east side. These were the gatekeepers from the camp of the Levites. (9:18).

In earlier times Phinehas son of Eleazar had been in charge of the gatekeepers, and the LORD was with him. (9:20).
Zechariah son of Meshelemiah was the gatekeeper at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. (9:21).

The number of those chosen to be gatekeepers at the thresholds was 212. They were registered by genealogy in their villages. David and Samuel the seer had appointed them to their positions of trust. (9:22).
So they and their descendants were assigned to guard the gates of the house of the LORD — the house called the Tent. (9:23).
The gatekeepers were stationed on the four sides: east, west, north, and south. (9:24).

They would spend the night stationed around the house of God, because they were responsible for guarding it and opening it every morning. (9:27).

And some of the sons of the priests mixed the spices. (9:30).

Those who were musicians, the heads of Levite families, stayed in the temple chambers and were exempt from other duties because they were on duty day and night. (9:33).
All these were heads of Levite families, chiefs according to their genealogies, and they lived in Jerusalem. (9:34).
Jeiel the father of Gibeon lived in Gibeon. His wife’s name was Maacah. (9:35).
Abdon was his firstborn son, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab, (9:36).
Gedor, Ahio, Zechariah, and Mikloth. (9:37).
Mikloth was the father of Shimeam. They too lived alongside their relatives in Jerusalem. (9:38).
Ner was the father of Kish, Kish was the father of Saul, and Saul was the father of Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab, and Esh-baal. (9:39).
The son of Jonathan: Merib-baal, who was the father of Micah. (9:40).
The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tahrea, and Ahaz. (9:41).

crossRefs: Nehemiah 11:3-24: The same register of families who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile.
Ezra 2:1-70: The list of exiles who came up with Zerubbabel, counted by family and by town.
2 Kings 25:8-12: Nebuzaradan burns the temple and the palace, breaks down the walls, and carries Judah away.
Numbers 3:25-37: The Gershonite, Kohathite, and Merarite charges over the tent, the ark, and its frames.
1 Chronicles 26:1-19: The gatekeepers assigned by lot to the east, north, south, and west gates.

translationNotes.note: Verse 2 lists four groups back in their towns: Israelites, priests, Levites, and temple servants. The last name means the ones handed over, a hereditary body of non-Levites assigned to the heavy work of the sanctuary. Ezra 8:20 says David and his officials set them apart to attend the Levites, and Joshua 9:23-27 puts the Gibeonites under exactly that sentence, cutting wood and drawing water for the house of God.

Verses 2-17 and Nehemiah 11:3-19 record the same resettlement of Jerusalem, with the same families and several of the same men, including the gatekeepers Shallum, Akkub, and Talmon. The two lists differ in detail. Chronicles counts Ephraim and Manasseh among those living in the city (verse 3) where Nehemiah names only Judah and Benjamin, and Chronicles gives 212 gatekeepers (verse 22) where Nehemiah 11:19 gives 172. Both stand as written.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֶחֶם הַפָּנִים (lechem ha-panim), bread of the face
translationNotes.note: Verse 32 assigns Kohathites to prepare 'the rows of the showbread every Sabbath.' Leviticus 24:5-9 sets out twelve loaves in two rows of six on the gold table, with frankincense alongside, replaced every sabbath, and the loaves taken off went to the priests to eat in a holy place. That is the bread David asked for and ate at Nob (1 Samuel 21:1-6), which Jesus cites at Mark 2:25-26.

Verse 30 says some of the priests' sons mixed the spices. The incense was a fixed formula, stacte, onycha, galbanum, and pure frankincense, salted and beaten fine (Exodus 30:34-38), and the same passage forbids anyone making it for their own use on pain of being cut off from the people. Compounding it was a priestly job, not a storekeeper's.

A milky white resin tapped from Boswellia trees in southern Arabia and Somaliland, carried north by caravan and worth its weight in trade. Verse 29 has it stored in the temple chambers with the fine flour, wine, and oil, under Levites who counted it in and out. It burned on the incense altar (Exodus 30:34) and went on top of every grain offering (Leviticus 2:1-2).

stories.keyTakeaway: After the exile to Babylon, Israelites resettle in their towns; the passage lists the genealogies and duties of those from Judah, Benjamin, the priests, Levites, and gatekeepers who returned to Jerusalem, along with descendants of Saul's family living in Gibeon.

stories.title: ⚔️ 1 Chronicles 10
summaryBullets: Now the Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before them, and many fell slain on Mount Gilboa. (10:1).
The Philistines followed hard after Saul and his sons, and they killed Saul’s sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua. (10:2).
When the battle intensified against Saul, the archers overtook him and wounded him. (10:3).

Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, “Draw your sword and run me through with it, or these uncircumcised men will come and torture me!” But his armor-bearer was terrified and refused to do it. So Saul took his own sword and fell on it. (10:4).
When his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he too fell on his own sword and died. (10:5).
So Saul died together with his three sons and all his house. (10:6).

When all the Israelites in the valley saw that the army had fled and that Saul and his sons had died, they abandoned their cities and ran away. So the Philistines came and occupied their cities. (10:7).
The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the dead, they found Saul and his sons fallen on Mount Gilboa. (10:8).
They stripped Saul, cut off his head, took his armor, and sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines to proclaim the news in the temple of their idols and among their people. (10:9).
They put his armor in the temple of their gods and hung his head in the temple of Dagon. (10:10).
When all the people of Jabesh-gilead heard about everything the Philistines had done to Saul, (10:11).
all their men of valor set out and retrieved the bodies of Saul and his sons and brought them to Jabesh. And they buried their bones under the oak in Jabesh and fasted seven days. (10:12).
So Saul died for his unfaithfulness to the LORD, because he did not keep the word of the LORD and even consulted a medium for guidance, (10:13).
and he failed to inquire of the LORD. So the LORD put him to death and turned the kingdom over to David son of Jesse. (10:14).

Deuteronomy 18:9-12: Ban on divination and mediums.
1 Samuel 15:23: Rejection of God’s word likened to divination.
2 Samuel 1:17-27: David’s lament for Saul and Jonathan.
Acts 13:21-22: Saul’s rejection contrasted with David’s rise.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אוֹב (ʾov), Greek: ἐγγαστρίμυθος (engastrimythos), Aramaic: אוּבָא (ʾuvāʾ)
translationNotes.note: Spirit-consultant/necromancer; expressly forbidden.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָעַל (maʿal), Greek: ἀπιστία/ἀσέβεια (apistia/asebeia), Aramaic: מעל (maʿal)
translationNotes.note: Breach of trust against covenant obligations.

A ridge rising to about 1,700 feet on the southeast rim of the Jezreel Valley, roughly fifty miles north of Jerusalem. The valley below is the one open corridor across northern Israel, wide and flat, which is exactly the ground Philistine chariots could use and Israel could not. Saul had to fight there, and the archers on the slope broke his line (verse 3).

The chief god of the Philistine cities, whose temples stood at Ashdod, Gaza, and Beth-shan. The name is tied to dagan, grain, and his worship was a fertility cult of the harvest. Verse 10 has Saul's head fastened up in Dagon's temple, which reverses 1 Samuel 5:1-5, where Dagon's own image fell on its face before the captured ark and broke its head and hands off on the threshold.

A town east of the Jordan in Gilead, about twenty miles south of the Sea of Galilee, and a night's hard march from Beth-shan where the Philistines displayed the bodies. The men of Jabesh went because Saul's first act as king had been to march all night and break Nahash the Ammonite's siege of their town (1 Samuel 11:1-11). They buried his bones under the oak and fasted seven days.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Philistines rout Israel on Mount Gilboa, kill Saul’s sons, and wound Saul, who falls on his own sword; they hang his head in the temple of Dagon until the men of Jabesh-gilead retrieve and bury the bones. Saul dies for his unfaithfulness, because he did not keep the word of the LORD and consulted a medium, so the LORD turns the kingdom over to David son of Jesse.

stories.title: 👑 1 Chronicles 11
summaryBullets: Then all Israel came together to David at Hebron and said, “Here we are, your own flesh and blood. (11:1).

Even in times past, while Saul was king, you were the one who led Israel out and brought them back. And the LORD your God said, ‘You will shepherd My people Israel, and you will be ruler over them.’” (11:2).

So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, where David made a covenant with them before the LORD. And they anointed him king over Israel, according to the word of the LORD through Samuel. (11:3).
Then David and all the Israelites marched to Jerusalem (that is, Jebus), where the Jebusites inhabited the land. (11:4).
The people of Jebus said to David, “You will never get in here.” Nevertheless , David captured the fortress of Zion (that is, the City of David). (11:5).
Now David had said, “Whoever is the first to strike down a Jebusite will become chief commander.” And Joab son of Zeruiah went up first, and he became the chief. (11:6).
So David took up residence in the fortress; that is why it was called the City of David. (11:7).
He built up the city around it, from the supporting terraces to the surrounding wall, while Joab restored the rest of the city. (11:8).
And David became greater and greater, for the LORD of Hosts was with him. (11:9).
Now these were the chiefs of David’s mighty men, who, together with all Israel, bolstered and strengthened his kingdom, according to the word of the LORD concerning Israel. (11:10).
This is the list of David’s mighty men: Jashobeam son of Hachmoni was chief of the officers; he wielded his spear against three hundred men, whom he killed at one time. (11:11).
Next in command was Eleazar son of Dodo the Ahohite, one of the three mighty men. (11:12).
He was with David at Pas-dammim when the Philistines gathered there for battle. At a place with a field full of barley, the troops fled from the Philistines. (11:13).
But Eleazar and David stationed themselves in the middle of the field and defended it. They struck down the Philistines, and the LORD brought about a great victory. (11:14).
Three of the thirty chief men went down to David, to the rock at the cave of Adullam, while a company of Philistines was encamped in the Valley of Rephaim. (11:15).
At that time David was in the stronghold, and the garrison of the Philistines was at Bethlehem. (11:16).
David longed for water and said, “Oh, that someone would get me a drink of water from the well near the gate of Bethlehem!” (11:17).

So the Three broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the well at the gate of Bethlehem, and brought it back to David. But he refused to drink it; instead , he poured it out to the LORD, (11:18).

saying, “Far be it from me, my God, to do this! How can I drink the blood of these men who risked their lives?” Because they had brought it at the risk of their lives, David refused to drink it. Such were the exploits of the three mighty men. (11:19).
Now Abishai, the brother of Joab, was chief of the Three, and he wielded his spear against three hundred men, killed them, and won a name along with the Three. (11:20).
He was doubly honored above the Three, and he became their commander, even though he was not included among the Three. (11:21).
And Benaiah son of Jehoiada was a man of valor from Kabzeel, a man of many exploits. He struck down two champions of Moab, and on a snowy day he went down into a pit and killed a lion. (11:22).

He also struck down an Egyptian, a huge man five cubits tall. Although the Egyptian had a spear like a weaver’s beam in his hand, Benaiah went against him with a club, snatched the spear from his hand, and killed the Egyptian with his own spear. (11:23).
These were the exploits of Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who won a name along with the three mighty men. (11:24).
He was most honored among the Thirty, but he did not become one of the Three. And David appointed him over his guard. (11:25).
Now these were the mighty men: Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan son of Dodo of Bethlehem, (11:26).
Shammoth the Harorite, Helez the Pelonite, (11:27).
Ira son of Ikkesh the Tekoite, Abiezer the Anathothite, (11:28).
Sibbecai the Hushathite, Ilai the Ahohite, (11:29).
Maharai the Netophathite, Heled son of Baanah the Netophathite, (11:30).
Ithai son of Ribai from Gibeah of the Benjamites, Benaiah the Pirathonite, (11:31).
Hurai from the brooks of Gaash, Abiel the Arbathite, (11:32).
Azmaveth the Baharumite, Eliahba the Shaalbonite, (11:33).
the sons of Hashem the Gizonite, Jonathan son of Shagee the Hararite, (11:34).
Ahiam son of Sachar the Hararite, Eliphal son of Ur, (11:35).
Hepher the Mecherathite, Ahijah the Pelonite, (11:36).
Hezro the Carmelite, Naarai son of Ezbai, (11:37).
Joel the brother of Nathan, Mibhar son of Hagri, (11:38).

Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite, (11:40).
Uriah the Hittite, Zabad son of Ahlai, (11:41).

Hanan son of Maacah, Joshaphat the Mithnite, (11:43).

crossRefs: 2 Samuel 5:1-10: The same anointing at Hebron and the same capture of the stronghold of Zion.
2 Samuel 23:8-39: The parallel roll of David's mighty men, the Three and the Thirty, with their deeds.
Joshua 15:63: Judah could not drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem, and they lived there alongside Judah.
Judges 1:21: Benjamin likewise failed to dislodge the Jebusites, who stayed in Jerusalem to that day.
1 Samuel 16:1-13: Samuel anoints David at Bethlehem years before any tribe accepts him as king.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גִּבּוֹרִים (gibborim), Greek: δυνατοί (dynatoi), Aramaic: גבוריא (gibboraya)
translationNotes.note: Heroes of war and valor; David’s elite warriors.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עִיר דָּוִיד (ʿIr David), Greek: πόλις Δαυίδ (polis Dauid), Aramaic: קרת דוד (qart David)
translationNotes.note: The fortress of Zion/Jerusalem after David conquered it.

Far more than an entrance; the public square where elders heard legal cases, contracts were witnessed, market business transacted, and news was exchanged. 'Sitting in the gate' (Genesis 19:1; Ruth 4:1-11; Proverbs 31:23) signals civic authority and active community life.

Verse 8 says David built the city 'from the Millo all around.' The word means the Filling. Jerusalem's eastern slope is steep, so building on it required packed earth and stone terraces held by retaining walls to make level ground. Later kings kept repairing it (1 Kings 9:15, 2 Chronicles 32:5).

David's army had two named ranks of honour, not a general officer corps. The Three were the top tier, and the Thirty a larger standing company of proven men whose membership changed as men died and were replaced. Entry was by a specific deed recorded against the man's name, which is why this chapter reads as a list of single feats.

stories.keyTakeaway: All Israel anoints David king at Hebron, and he captures Jerusalem from the Jebusites with Joab as his commander; the chapter then lists David's mighty warriors and their exploits.

they were archers using both the right and left hands to sling stones and shoot arrows; and they were Saul’s kinsmen from Benjamin): (12:2).
Ahiezer their chief and Joash, who were the sons of Shemaah the Gibeathite; Jeziel and Pelet, the sons of Azmaveth; Beracah; Jehu the Anathothite; (12:3).
