Johanan the eighth, Elzabad the ninth, (12:12).
Jeremiah the tenth, and Machbanai the eleventh. (12:13).
These Gadites were army commanders, the least of whom was a match for a hundred, and the greatest for a thousand. (12:14).
These are the ones who crossed the Jordan in the first month when it was overflowing all its banks, and they put to flight all those in the valleys, both to the east and to the west. (12:15).
Other Benjamites and some men from Judah also came to David in his stronghold. (12:16).

And David went out to meet them, saying, “If you have come to me in peace to help me, my heart will be united with you; but if you have come to betray me to my enemies when my hands are free of violence, may the God of our fathers see it and judge you.” (12:17).

Then the Spirit came upon Amasai, the chief of the Thirty, and he said: “We are yours, O David! We are with you, O son of Jesse! Peace, peace to you, and peace to your helpers, for your God helps you.” So David received them and made them leaders of his troops. (12:18).

Some from Manasseh defected to David when he went with the Philistines to fight against Saul. (They did not help the Philistines because the Philistine rulers consulted and sent David away, saying, “It will cost us our heads if he defects to his master Saul.”) (12:19).
When David went to Ziklag, these men of Manasseh defected to him: Adnah, Jozabad, Jediael, Michael, Jozabad, Elihu, and Zillethai, chiefs of thousands in Manasseh. (12:20).
They helped David against the raiders, for they were all mighty men of valor and commanders in the army. (12:21).
For at that time men came to David day after day to help him, until he had a great army, like the army of God. (12:22).
Now these are the numbers of men armed for battle who came to David at Hebron to turn Saul’s kingdom over to him, in accordance with the word of the LORD: (12:23).
From Judah: 6,800 armed troops bearing shields and spears. (12:24).
From Simeon: 7,100 mighty men of valor, ready for battle. (12:25).
including Jehoiada, leader of the house of Aaron, with 3,700 men, (12:27).
and Zadok, a mighty young man of valor, with 22 commanders from his own family. (12:28).
From Benjamin, the kinsmen of Saul: 3,000, most of whom had remained loyal to the house of Saul up to that time. (12:29).
From Ephraim: 20,800 mighty men of valor, famous among their own clans. (12:30).
From the half-tribe of Manasseh: 18,000 designated by name to come and make David king. (12:31).
From Issachar, men who understood the times and knew what Israel should do: 200 chiefs with all their kinsmen at their command. (12:32).
From Zebulun: 50,000 fit for service, trained for battle with all kinds of weapons of war, who with one purpose were devoted to David. (12:33).
From Naphtali: 1,000 commanders, accompanied by 37,000 men with shield and spear. (12:34).
From Dan: 28,600 prepared for battle. (12:35).
From Asher: 40,000 fit for service, prepared for battle. (12:36).
And from east of the Jordan, from Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh there: 120,000 armed with every kind of weapon of war. (12:37).
All these men of war, arrayed for battle, came to Hebron fully determined to make David king over all Israel. And all the rest of the Israelites were of one mind to make David king. (12:38).
They spent three days there eating and drinking with David, for their relatives had provided for them. (12:39).

And their neighbors from as far away as Issachar, Zebulun, and Naphtali came bringing food on donkeys, camels, mules, and oxen— abundant supplies of flour, fig cakes and raisin cakes, wine and oil, oxen and sheep. Indeed, there was joy in Israel. (12:40).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 27:1-7: Achish king of Gath gives David the town of Ziklag, where these men came over to him.
1 Samuel 22:1-2: Four hundred men in distress, in debt, and bitter gather to David at the cave of Adullam.
1 Samuel 29:1-11: The Philistine commanders refuse to let David fight at Aphek and send him back.
1 Samuel 30:1-20: David pursues the Amalekites who burned Ziklag and recovers everything taken.
2 Samuel 5:1-5: All the tribes come to David at Hebron and anoint him king over Israel.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גִּבּוֹרִים (gibborim), Greek: δυνατοί (dynatoi), Aramaic: גבוריא (gibboraya)
translationNotes.note: Heroes of war and valor; David’s elite warriors.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עִיר דָּוִיד (ʿIr David), Greek: πόλις Δαυίδ (polis Dauid), Aramaic: קרת דוד (qart David)
translationNotes.note: The fortress of Zion/Jerusalem after David conquered it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יוֹדְעֵי בִינָה לַעִתִּים (yodʿei binah laʿittim), Greek: συνετοὶ εἰς καιρούς (synetoi eis kairous), Aramaic: ידעי חכמת זמנין (yodʿei ḥokhmat zmanin)
translationNotes.note: Phrase describing Issachar’s discernment; wisdom in recognizing God’s timing and proper action.

A town in the dry Negev country south of Gath, handed to David by the Philistine king Achish while Saul hunted him. David held it a year and four months (1 Samuel 27:7), raiding desert peoples and reporting the plunder as though it came from Judah. It is where these defectors found him, outside Saul's reach.

stories.keyTakeaway: Warriors from multiple tribes defect to David at Ziklag and his stronghold, swearing loyalty to him; later, armed men from all twelve tribes gather at Hebron, fully committed to making him king over Israel.

headings.text: The Mighty Men Join David at Ziklag

stories.title: 🛕 1 Chronicles 13
summaryBullets: Then David conferred with all his leaders, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds. (13:1).

And he said to the whole assembly of Israel, “If it seems good to you, and if this is of the LORD our God, let us send word far and wide to the rest of our brothers in all the land of Israel, and also to the priests and Levites in their cities and pasturelands, so that they may join us. (13:2).
Then let us bring back the ark of our God, for we did not inquire of Him in the days of Saul.” (13:3).
And because this proposal seemed right to all the people, the whole assembly agreed to it. (13:4).
So David assembled all Israel, from the River Shihor in Egypt to Lebo-hamath, to bring the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim. (13:5).

David and all Israel went up to Baalah of Judah (that is, Kiriath-jearim) to bring up from there the ark of God the LORD, who is enthroned between the cherubim — the ark that is called by the Name. (13:6).
So they carried the ark of God from the house of Abinadab on a new cart, with Uzzah and Ahio guiding the cart. (13:7).
David and all the Israelites were celebrating before God with all their might, with songs and on harps and lyres, with tambourines, cymbals, and trumpets. (13:8).
When they came to the threshing floor of Chidon, Uzzah reached out and took hold of the ark, because the oxen had stumbled. (13:9).
And the anger of the LORD burned against Uzzah, and He struck him down because he had put his hand on the ark. So he died there before God. (13:10).
Then David became angry because the LORD had burst forth against Uzzah. So he named that place Perez-uzzah, as it is called to this day. (13:11).
That day David feared God and asked, “How can I ever bring the ark of God to me?” (13:12).
So he did not move the ark with him to the City of David; instead, he took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. (13:13).
Thus the ark of God remained with the family of Obed-edom in his house for three months, and the LORD blessed his household and everything he owned. (13:14).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 6:1-11: The same procession from Baale-judah, the death of Uzzah, and the three months at Obed-edom's house.
Numbers 4:15: The Kohathites carry the holy things only after Aaron covers them, and must not touch them or they die.
Exodus 25:12-15: Poles are set in the rings of the ark and are never to be taken out of them.
1 Samuel 6:7-12: The Philistines send the ark home on a new cart drawn by two milk cows.
1 Samuel 7:1-2: The ark is brought to Abinadab's house at Kiriath-jearim and stays there twenty years.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲרוֹן הַבְּרִית (aron habberit), Greek: κιβωτὸς τῆς διαθήκης (kibōtos tēs diathēkēs), Aramaic: ארונא דקיימא (arona d’qayyama)
translationNotes.note: Sacred chest containing the tablets of the covenant, symbolizing God’s throne and presence.

A flat, hard, outdoor surface, usually a leveled rock or beaten-earth circle at the edge of town, where harvested grain was separated from chaff. Oxen pulled a wooden sledge over the stalks; the mixed kernels and chaff were then winnowed in the wind. Threshing floors doubled as public civic spaces (Ruth 3; 2 Samuel 24:18; Solomon's temple site).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קִרְיַת יְעָרִים (Qiryat Yearim), city of forests
translationNotes.note: A town on the wooded ridge about nine miles west of Jerusalem, on the road up from the coastal plain. The ark sat in a private house there for twenty years after the Philistines returned it (1 Samuel 7:1-2), which means Israel had a tabernacle at one place and the ark at another for a generation.

The ark was built with rings at its corners and two poles run through them that were never to be removed (Exodus 25:12-15), so that Levites could carry it on their shoulders and no hand ever touched the chest. Verse 7 puts it on a new cart instead, which is how the Philistines had shipped it (1 Samuel 6:7). When the oxen stumbled, Uzza reached out to steady it and died.

stories.keyTakeaway: David assembles all Israel to bring the ark of God from Kiriath Jearim to Jerusalem, but when Uzzah steadies the ark as the oxen stumble, God strikes him dead; David leaves the ark at Obed-Edom's house instead.

stories.title: 🛕 1 Chronicles 14
summaryBullets: Now Hiram king of Tyre sent envoys to David, along with cedar logs, stonemasons, and carpenters, to build a palace for him. (14:1).
And David realized that the LORD had established him as king over Israel and had highly exalted his kingdom for the sake of His people Israel. (14:2).
And David took more wives in Jerusalem and became the father of more sons and daughters. (14:3).
These are the names of the children born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon, (14:4).
Ibhar, Elishua, Elpelet, (14:5).
Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia, (14:6).
Elishama, Beeliada, and Eliphelet. (14:7).
When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over all Israel, they all went in search of him; but David learned of this and went out to face them. (14:8).
Now the Philistines had come and raided the Valley of Rephaim. (14:9).
So David inquired of God, “Should I go up against the Philistines? Will You deliver them into my hand?” “Go,” replied the LORD, “for I will deliver them into your hand.” (14:10).

So David and his men went up to Baal-perazim, where he defeated the Philistines and said, “Like a bursting flood, God has burst out against my enemies by my hand.” So they called that place Baal-perazim. (14:11).
There the Philistines abandoned their gods, and David ordered that they be burned in the fire. (14:12).
Once again the Philistines raided the valley. (14:13).
So David again inquired of God, who answered him, “Do not march up after them, but circle around them and attack them in front of the balsam trees. (14:14).
As soon as you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, move out to battle, because this will mean that God has gone out before you to strike the camp of the Philistines.” (14:15).
So David did as God had commanded him, and they struck down the army of the Philistines all the way from Gibeon to Gezer. (14:16).
And David’s fame went out into every land, and the LORD caused all nations to fear him. (14:17).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 5:11-25: The same palace built by Tyre, the same sons born in Jerusalem, and the same two Philistine battles.
1 Kings 5:1-11: Hiram of Tyre supplies Solomon with cedar and cypress logs floated down the coast.
Deuteronomy 7:5,25: Israel is to burn the carved images of the nations' gods rather than keep the silver and gold on them.
1 Chronicles 3:5-8: The sons born to David in Jerusalem listed again by name.
Isaiah 28:21: Isaiah recalls the LORD rising up as at Mount Perazim to do His strange work.

translationNotes.note: A Phoenician port about a hundred miles north of Jerusalem, built partly on an island, the trading capital of the Lebanese coast. Its forests supplied the cedar no Israelite hill could grow, and its masons and carpenters had the stone and timber skills Israel lacked. Hiram's help here is the start of a working alliance that later builds Solomon's temple.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בַּעַל פְּרָצִים (Baal Peratsim), lord of breakings-through
translationNotes.note: David names the site for what happened there. In verse 11 he says God 'has broken through my enemies by my hand like a bursting flood,' using the verb parats, to burst out, and the place takes its name from it. English keeps the name and loses the wordplay.

A broad grain-growing valley running southwest from Jerusalem toward Bethlehem, level enough for chariots and the natural approach to the city from Philistine territory. Isaiah 17:5 uses its harvest as a picture of reaping. Twice in this chapter the Philistines deploy there, and twice David asks God before he moves.

Verse 15 tells David to attack when he hears marching in the tops of the trees. The Hebrew word is used only here and in the parallel at 2 Samuel 5:23-24, and the tree is not certainly identified; balsam or mulberry are the usual renderings. What the text is clear about is the signal: the sound in the treetops goes ahead of him, and he moves on it.

stories.keyTakeaway: Hiram of Tyre sends materials to build David a palace, and David fathers multiple sons in Jerusalem; when the Philistines attack, David consults God, defeats them twice using God's guidance, and his fame spreads throughout the lands.

stories.title: 🛕 1 Chronicles 15
summaryBullets: David constructed buildings for himself in the City of David, and he prepared a place for the ark of God and pitched a tent for it. (15:1).
Then David said, “No one but the Levites may carry the ark of God, because the LORD has chosen them to carry the ark of the LORD and to minister before Him forever.” (15:2).
And David assembled all Israel in Jerusalem to bring up the ark of the LORD to the place he had prepared for it. (15:3).
Then he gathered together the descendants of Aaron and the Levites: (15:4).
From the Kohathites, Uriel the chief and 120 of his relatives; (15:5).
from the Merarites, Asaiah the chief and 220 of his relatives; (15:6).
from the Gershomites, Joel the chief and 130 of his relatives; (15:7).
from the Elizaphanites, Shemaiah the chief and 200 of his relatives; (15:8).
from the Hebronites, Eliel the chief and 80 of his relatives; (15:9).
and from the Uzzielites, Amminadab the chief and 112 of his relatives. (15:10).
David summoned the priests Zadok and Abiathar and the Levites Uriel, Asaiah, Joel, Shemaiah, Eliel, and Amminadab. (15:11).

And he said to them, “You are the heads of the Levitical families. You and your relatives must consecrate yourselves so that you may bring the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel, to the place I have prepared for it. (15:12).
It was because you Levites were not with us the first time that the LORD our God burst forth in anger against us. For we did not consult Him about the proper order.” (15:13).
So the priests and Levites consecrated themselves to bring up the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel. (15:14).
And the Levites carried the ark of God on their shoulders with the poles, as Moses had commanded in accordance with the word of the LORD. (15:15).
David also told the leaders of the Levites to appoint their relatives as singers to lift up their voices with joy, accompanied by musical instruments— harps, lyres, and cymbals. (15:16).
So the Levites appointed Heman son of Joel; from his brothers, Asaph son of Berechiah; from their brothers the Merarites, Ethan son of Kushaiah; (15:17).
and with them their brothers next in rank: Zechariah, Jaaziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, Mikneiah, and the gatekeepers Obed-edom and Jeiel. (15:18).
The musicians Heman, Asaph, and Ethan were to sound the bronze cymbals. (15:19).
Zechariah, Aziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Maaseiah, and Benaiah were to play the harps according to Alamoth. (15:20).
And Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, Mikneiah, Obed-edom, Jeiel, and Azaziah were to lead the music with lyres according to Sheminith. (15:21).
Chenaniah the head Levite was the director of the music because he was highly skilled. (15:22).
Berechiah and Elkanah were to be guardians of the ark. (15:23).

Shebaniah, Joshaphat, Nethanel, Amasai, Zechariah, Benaiah, and Eliezer — the priests — were to blow the trumpets before the ark of God. Obed-edom and Jehiah were also to be guardians of the ark. (15:24).
So David, the elders of Israel, and the commanders of thousands went with rejoicing to bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD from the house of Obed-edom. (15:25).
And because God helped the Levites who were carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD, they sacrificed seven bulls and seven rams. (15:26).

Now David was dressed in a robe of fine linen, as were all the Levites who were carrying the ark, as well as the singers and Chenaniah, the director of music for the singers. David also wore a linen ephod. (15:27).
So all Israel brought up the ark of the covenant of the LORD with shouting, with the sounding of rams’ horns and trumpets, and with cymbals and the music of harps and lyres. (15:28).

As the ark of the covenant of the LORD was entering the City of David, Saul’s daughter Michal looked down from a window and saw King David dancing and celebrating, and she despised him in her heart. (15:29).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 10:8: The LORD sets Levi apart to carry the ark of the covenant, to stand and minister, and to bless in His name.
Numbers 7:9: No carts are given to the Kohathites, because their charge is carried on the shoulder.
2 Samuel 6:12-23: The same procession with sacrifices and dancing, and Michal's contempt at the window.
Exodus 25:10-16: The ark's dimensions, its rings and poles, and the testimony placed inside it.
1 Samuel 18:20-27: Michal daughter of Saul is given to David for a bride price of a hundred Philistines.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲרוֹן הַבְּרִית (aron habberit), Greek: κιβωτὸς τῆς διαθήκης (kibōtos tēs diathēkēs), Aramaic: ארונא דקיימא (arona d’qayyama)
translationNotes.note: Sacred chest containing the tablets of the covenant, symbolizing God’s throne and presence.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵפוֹד (ʾefod), Greek: ἐπωμίς (epōmis), Aramaic: אפוד (epod)
translationNotes.note: Priestly garment; David wore a linen ephod in humility and devotion during worship.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְכַרְכֵּר (mekharker), Greek: ὀρχέομαι (orcheomai), Aramaic: רקד (raqed)
translationNotes.note: Joyful whirling dance before the LORD; an embodied act of worship.

A male descendant of Levi (excluding the Aaronic priestly line). Assisted the priests in temple service: music, gatekeeping, instructing the people, preparing sacrifices. The priest and Levite who pass by the wounded man in the Good Samaritan parable (Luke 10:31-32) make Jesus' point cut sharper; both were professionally obligated to help.

Verse 27 has David wearing a linen ephod in the procession. This is not the jewelled high priestly vestment of Exodus 28 but a plain sleeveless linen garment worn by those serving before the LORD; the boy Samuel wore one (1 Samuel 2:18). David is dressed as a servant at the sanctuary, not as a king, which is what Michal despises.

stories.keyTakeaway: David assembles Levites and musicians to bring the ark of God to Jerusalem with proper ceremony, assigning specific roles for carrying, playing instruments, and sounding trumpets. The ark enters the City of David amid celebration while Michal watches David dance and despises him.

headings.text: The Priests and Levites Carry the Ark

stories.title: 🛕 1 Chronicles 16
summaryBullets: So they brought the ark of God and placed it inside the tent that David had pitched for it. And they presented burnt offerings and peace offerings before God. (16:1).
When David had finished sacrificing the burnt offerings and peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD. (16:2).
Then he distributed to every man and woman of Israel a loaf of bread, a date cake, and a raisin cake. (16:3).
David appointed some of the Levites to minister before the ark of the LORD, to celebrate, to give thanks, and to praise the LORD, the God of Israel. (16:4).

Asaph was the chief, Zechariah was second, then Jeiel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Mattithiah, Eliab, Benaiah, Obed-edom, and Jeiel. They were to play the harps and lyres, while Asaph sounded the cymbals (16:5).
and the priests Benaiah and Jahaziel blew the trumpets regularly before the ark of the covenant of God. (16:6).
On that day David first committed to Asaph and his associates this song of thanksgiving to the LORD: (16:7).
“Give thanks to the LORD; call upon His name; make known His deeds among the nations. (16:8).
Sing to Him, sing praises to Him; tell of all His wonders. (16:9).
Glory in His holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice. (16:10).
Seek out the LORD and His strength; seek His face always. (16:11).
Remember the wonders He has done, His marvels, and the judgments He has pronounced, (16:12).
O offspring of His servant Israel, O sons of Jacob, His chosen ones. (16:13).
He is the LORD our God; His judgments carry throughout the earth. (16:14).
Remember His covenant forever, the word He ordained for a thousand generations— (16:15).
the covenant He made with Abraham, and the oath He swore to Isaac. (16:16).
He confirmed it to Jacob as a decree, to Israel as an everlasting covenant: (16:17).
‘I will give you the land of Canaan as the portion of your inheritance.’ (16:18).
When they were few in number, few indeed, and strangers in the land, (16:19).
they wandered from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another. (16:20).
He let no man oppress them; He rebuked kings on their behalf: (16:21).
‘Do not touch My anointed ones! Do no harm to My prophets!’ (16:22).
Sing to the LORD, all the earth. Proclaim His salvation day after day. (16:23).
Declare His glory among the nations, His wonders among all peoples. (16:24).
For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; He is to be feared above all gods. (16:25).
For all the gods of the nations are idols, but it is the LORD who made the heavens. (16:26).
Splendor and majesty are before Him; strength and joy fill His dwelling. (16:27).
Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the nations, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength. (16:28).
Ascribe to the LORD the glory due His name; bring an offering and come before Him. Worship the LORD in the splendor of His holiness; (16:29).
tremble before Him, all the earth. The world is firmly established; it cannot be moved. (16:30).
Let the heavens be glad, and the earth rejoice. Let them say among the nations, ‘The LORD reigns!’ (16:31).
Let the sea resound, and all that fills it; let the fields exult, and all that is in them. (16:32).
Then the trees of the forest will sing for joy before the LORD, for He is coming to judge the earth. (16:33).
Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever. (16:34).
Then cry out: ‘Save us, O God of our salvation; gather and deliver us from the nations, that we may give thanks to Your holy name, that we may glory in Your praise.’ (16:35).
Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting.” Then all the people said, “Amen!” and “Praise the LORD!” (16:36).
So David left Asaph and his associates there before the ark of the covenant of the LORD, to minister there regularly according to the daily requirements, (16:37).
along with Obed-edom and his sixty-eight relatives. Obed-edom son of Jeduthun, and also Hosah, were to be gatekeepers. (16:38).
And David left Zadok the priest and his fellow priests before the tabernacle of the LORD at the high place in Gibeon (16:39).

to regularly present burnt offerings to the LORD on the altar of burnt offerings, morning and evening, according to all that was written in the Law of the LORD, which He had commanded Israel to keep. (16:40).
With them were Heman, Jeduthun, and the rest of those chosen and designated by name to give thanks to the LORD, for “His loving devotion endures forever.” (16:41).
Heman and Jeduthun had with them trumpets and cymbals for the music and instruments for the songs of God. And the sons of Jeduthun were stationed at the gate. (16:42).
Then all the people departed for their homes, and David returned home to bless his household. (16:43).
crossRefs: Psalm 105:1-15: The opening section of David's song of thanks, standing there word for word.
Psalm 96:1-13: The middle section, the call to sing a new song and declare His glory among the nations.
Psalm 106:1,47-48: The closing verses, with the plea to gather Israel from among the nations.
2 Samuel 6:17-19: The same offerings, and a loaf, a portion of meat, and a raisin cake given to every Israelite.
1 Kings 3:4: The great high place at Gibeon, where the altar stood and Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲרוֹן הַבְּרִית (aron habberit), Greek: κιβωτὸς τῆς διαθήκης (kibōtos tēs diathēkēs), Aramaic: ארונא דקיימא (arona d’qayyama)
translationNotes.note: Sacred chest containing the tablets of the covenant, symbolizing God’s throne and presence.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְכַרְכֵּר (mekharker), Greek: ὀρχέομαι (orcheomai), Aramaic: רקד (raqed)
translationNotes.note: Joyful whirling dance before the LORD; an embodied act of worship.

Far more than an entrance; the public square where elders heard legal cases, contracts were witnessed, market business transacted, and news was exchanged. 'Sitting in the gate' (Genesis 19:1; Ruth 4:1-11; Proverbs 31:23) signals civic authority and active community life.

A town about six miles northwest of Jerusalem. Verses 39-40 leave Zadok and the regular burnt offerings there while the ark goes to David's tent in Jerusalem, so for a generation Israel had the tabernacle and altar at one site and the ark at another (2 Chronicles 1:3-6). Gibeon is the town whose people tricked Joshua into a treaty with worn sandals and mouldy bread (Joshua 9:3-15).

stories.keyTakeaway: David places the ark in a tent, sacrifices offerings, and distributes bread to the people; he appoints Levites led by Asaph to minister before it with music and praise, then establishes priests at Gibeon to offer sacrifices regularly.

headings.text: Sing to the Lord, All the Earth

stories.title: 📜 1 Chronicles 17
summaryBullets: After David had settled into his palace, he said to Nathan the prophet, “Here I am, living in a house of cedar, while the ark of the covenant of the LORD is under a tent.” (17:1).
And Nathan replied to David, “Do all that is in your heart, for God is with you.” (17:2).
But that night the word of God came to Nathan, saying, (17:3).
“Go and tell My servant David that this is what the LORD says: You are not the one to build Me a house in which to dwell. (17:4).
For I have not dwelt in a house from the day I brought Israel up out of Egypt until this day, but I have moved from tent to tent and dwelling to dwelling. (17:5).
In all My journeys with all the Israelites, have I ever asked any of the leaders I appointed to shepherd My people, ‘Why haven’t you built Me a house of cedar?’ (17:6).
Now then, you are to tell My servant David that this is what the LORD of Hosts says: I took you from the pasture, from following the flock, to be the ruler over My people Israel. (17:7).
I have been with you wherever you have gone, and I have cut off all your enemies from before you. Now I will make for you a name like that of the greatest in the land. (17:8).

And I will provide a place for My people Israel and will plant them so that they may dwell in a place of their own and be disturbed no more. No longer will the sons of wickedness oppress them as they did at the beginning (17:9).
and have done since the day I appointed judges over My people Israel. And I will subdue all your enemies. Moreover , I declare to you that the LORD will build a house for you. (17:10).
And when your days are fulfilled and you go to be with your fathers, I will raise up your descendant after you, one of your own sons, and I will establish his kingdom. (17:11).
He will build a house for Me, and I will establish his throne forever. (17:12).
I will be his Father, and he will be My son. And I will never remove My loving devotion from him as I removed it from your predecessor. (17:13).
But I will set him over My house and My kingdom forever, and his throne will be established forever.” (17:14).
So Nathan relayed to David all the words of this entire revelation. (17:15).
Then King David went in, sat before the LORD, and said, “Who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far? (17:16).
And as if this was a small thing in Your eyes, O God, You have spoken about the future of the house of Your servant and have regarded me as a man of great distinction, O LORD God. (17:17).
What more can David say to You for honoring Your servant? For You know Your servant, (17:18).
O LORD. For the sake of Your servant and according to Your own heart, You have accomplished this great thing and made known all these great promises. (17:19).
O LORD, there is none like You, and there is no God but You, according to everything we have heard with our own ears. (17:20).

And who is like Your people Israel — the one nation on earth whom God went out to redeem as a people for Himself? You made a name for Yourself through great and awesome wonders by driving out nations from before Your people, whom You redeemed from Egypt. (17:21).
For You have made Your people Israel Your very own forever, and You, O LORD, have become their God. (17:22).
And now, O LORD, let the word You have spoken concerning Your servant and his house be established forever. Do as You have promised, (17:23).

so that Your name will be established and magnified forever when it is said, ‘The LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, is God over Israel.’ And may the house of Your servant David be established before You. (17:24).
For You, my God, have revealed to Your servant that You will build a house for him. Therefore Your servant has found the courage to pray before You. (17:25).
And now, O LORD, You are God! And You have promised this goodness to Your servant. (17:26).
So now You have been pleased to bless the house of Your servant, that it may continue forever before You. For You, O LORD, have blessed it, and it will be blessed forever.” (17:27).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 7: Parallel account of the covenant.
Psalm 89:3-4: God’s covenant with David’s house.
Isaiah 9:6-7: Promise of a son on David’s throne forever.
Luke 1:32-33: Angel Gabriel: Jesus will inherit David’s throne eternally.
Acts 15:16: Restoration of David’s fallen tent through Christ.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בַּיִת (bayit), Greek: οἶκος (oikos), Aramaic: ביתא (bayta)
translationNotes.note: Double meaning: physical temple vs. dynasty. God flips David’s plan to show divine initiative.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עוֹלָם (ʿolam), Greek: αἰών (aiōn), Aramaic: עלמא (ʿalma)
translationNotes.note: Can mean 'long duration' or 'eternity'; covenant promise stretches beyond Solomon to messianic fulfillment.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶרֶז (erez), cedar - יְרִיעָה (yeriah), tent curtain
translationNotes.note: David's complaint in verse 1 is a contrast in building materials. He lives in a house of cedar, imported timber that only a king could afford, while the ark sits under goat-hair tent curtains, the same portable covering Israel used in the wilderness. Nothing was wrong with the tent; it is the mismatch he cannot live with.

Verse 6 refers to the leaders God commanded to shepherd Israel before the monarchy. A shofet was not a courtroom official but a deliverer raised up for a crisis, who then led the region for the rest of his life, as Deborah, Gideon, and Samson did. The point of the verse is that God never once asked any of them for a house of cedar.

stories.keyTakeaway: David wants to build a house for the LORD, but the LORD answers through Nathan that He will build David a house: a son will build His house, and He will be his Father and establish his throne forever; David then sits before the LORD and prays, marveling at the promise and asking that it be established forever.

stories.title: ⚔️ 1 Chronicles 18
summaryBullets: Some time later, David defeated the Philistines, subdued them, and took Gath and its villages from the hand of the Philistines. (18:1).
David also defeated the Moabites, and they became subject to David and brought him tribute. (18:2).
As far as Hamath, David also defeated King Hadadezer of Zobah, who had marched out to establish his dominion along the Euphrates River. (18:3).
David captured from him a thousand chariots, seven thousand charioteers, and twenty thousand foot soldiers, and he hamstrung all the horses except a hundred he kept for the chariots. (18:4).
When the Arameans of Damascus came to help King Hadadezer of Zobah, David struck down twenty-two thousand of their men. (18:5).
Then he placed garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and the Arameans became subject to David and brought him tribute. So the LORD made David victorious wherever he went. (18:6).
And David took the gold shields that belonged to the officers of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem. (18:7).
And from Tibhath and Cun, cities of Hadadezer, David took a large amount of bronze, with which Solomon made the bronze Sea, the pillars, and various bronze articles. (18:8).
When King Tou of Hamath heard that David had defeated the entire army of Hadadezer king of Zobah, (18:9).

he sent his son Hadoram to greet King David and bless him for fighting and defeating Hadadezer, who had been at war with Tou. Hadoram brought all kinds of articles of gold and silver and bronze, (18:10).

and King David dedicated these to the LORD, along with the silver and gold he had carried off from all these nations — from Edom and Moab, and from the Ammonites, Philistines, and Amalekites. (18:11).
Moreover, Abishai son of Zeruiah struck down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt. (18:12).
He placed garrisons in Edom, and all the Edomites were subject to David. So the LORD made David victorious wherever he went. (18:13).
Thus David reigned over all Israel and administered justice and righteousness for all his people: (18:14).
Joab son of Zeruiah was over the army; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder; (18:15).
Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar were priests; Shavsha was the scribe; (18:16).
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and Pelethites; and David’s sons were chief officials at the king’s side. (18:17).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 8:1-18: The same campaigns against Philistia, Moab, Zobah, Aram, and Edom, and the same list of officials.
Deuteronomy 17:16: The king is not to multiply horses for himself or send the people back to Egypt to get them.
Joshua 11:6,9: Joshua hamstrings the horses of the northern kings and burns their chariots.
1 Kings 7:15-16,45-47: The bronze pillars, basins, and vessels Solomon made, of bronze too much to be weighed.
2 Samuel 12:30-31: The crown taken from Rabbah and the forced labour imposed on the Ammonite towns.

translationNotes.note: Originally professional copyists of Scripture. By the New Testament era, scholar-teachers of the Law; often, though not exclusively, aligned with the Pharisees. They formed the educated religious class that adjudicated everyday halakhic questions.

Verse 4 says David kept a hundred chariot teams and hamstrung the rest, cutting the tendon at the back of the hock so the animal could never pull again. Chariots were the tank of the age and the one weapon Israel's hill country could not support: they need level ground, trained teams, wheelwrights, and a supply chain. Cutting the horses denied the technology to the enemy without Israel adopting it.

Aram is the Semitic people of inland Syria, spread across small kingdoms rather than one state; Zobah was the strongest of them, north of Damascus in the Beqaa region. Their language, Aramaic, later became the common speech of the whole Near East and of Judea in Jesus' day. Hadadezer's name carries Hadad, the Aramean storm god.

Verses 2 and 6 say Moab and Aram 'brought tribute.' A defeated kingdom kept its own king and towns but paid an annual levy in silver, gold, livestock, or goods, and was counted a servant of the greater king. It was cheaper than occupation and normal practice across the ancient Near East; withholding it was how a vassal declared rebellion, as Moab does in 2 Kings 3:4-5.

stories.keyTakeaway: David defeats the Philistines, Moabites, Hadadezer's forces, and Edomites in a series of campaigns, establishing garrisons across conquered territories and receiving tribute and gifts from defeated kings. He dedicates the plunder to the Lord and rules Israel justly with his military and administrative officials.

stories.title: ⚔️ 1 Chronicles 19
summaryBullets: Some time later, Nahash king of the Ammonites died and was succeeded by his son. (19:1).

And David said, “I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, because his father showed kindness to me.” So David sent messengers to console Hanun concerning his father. But when David’s servants arrived in the land of the Ammonites to console him, (19:2).

the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun, “Just because David has sent you comforters, do you really believe he is showing respect for your father? Have not his servants come to you to explore the land, spy it out, and overthrow it?” (19:3).
So Hanun took David’s servants, shaved their beards, cut off their garments at the hips, and sent them away. (19:4).

When someone came and told David about his men, he sent messengers to meet them, since the men had been thoroughly humiliated. The king told them, “Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown back, and then return.” (19:5).

When the Ammonites realized that they had become a stench to David, Hanun and the Ammonites sent a thousand talents of silver to hire for themselves chariots and horsemen from Aram-naharaim, Aram-maacah, and Zobah. (19:6).

So they hired for themselves thirty-two thousand chariots, as well as the king of Maacah with his troops, who came and camped near Medeba while the Ammonites were mustered from their cities and marched out for battle. (19:7).
On hearing this, David sent Joab and the entire army of mighty men. (19:8).
The Ammonites marched out and arrayed themselves for battle at the entrance to the city, while the kings who had come stayed by themselves in the open country. (19:9).
When Joab saw the battle lines before him and behind him, he selected some of the best men of Israel and arrayed them against the Arameans. (19:10).
And he placed the rest of the troops under the command of his brother Abishai, who arrayed them against the Ammonites. (19:11).
“If the Arameans are too strong for me,” said Joab, “then you will come to my rescue. And if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will come to your rescue. (19:12).
Be strong and let us fight bravely for our people and for the cities of our God. May the LORD do what is good in His sight.” (19:13).
So Joab and his troops advanced to fight the Arameans, who fled before him. (19:14).
When the Ammonites saw that the Arameans had fled, they too fled before Joab’s brother Abishai, and they entered the city. So Joab went back to Jerusalem. (19:15).

When the Arameans saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they sent messengers to bring more Arameans from beyond the Euphrates, with Shophach the commander of Hadadezer’s army leading them. (19:16).

When this was reported to David, he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, advanced toward the Arameans, and arrayed for battle against them. When David lined up to engage them in battle, they fought against him. (19:17).
But the Arameans fled before Israel, and David killed seven thousand of their charioteers and forty thousand foot soldiers. He also killed Shophach the commander of their army. (19:18).
When Hadadezer’s subjects saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they made peace with David and became subject to him. So the Arameans were unwilling to help the Ammonites anymore. (19:19).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 10:1-19: The same insult to David's envoys and the same defeat of Ammon and their hired Arameans.
1 Samuel 11:1-11: Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh-gilead and demands the right eye of every man in it.
Deuteronomy 23:3-6: No Ammonite or Moabite is admitted to the assembly, because they hired Balaam against Israel.
Genesis 19:36-38: Lot's younger daughter bears Ben-ammi, the father of the Ammonites.
Leviticus 19:27: Israel is forbidden to round off the hair at the temples or mar the edges of the beard.

translationNotes.note: The largest unit of weight and money in the ancient world. A talent of silver weighed about 75 lbs (34 kg) and equaled roughly 6,000 denarii; about 20 years of a laborer's wages. A talent of gold was worth far more. When Jesus tells the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30), each talent represents a staggering trust.

About 75 lbs (34 kg) of metal. A 'talent of gold' in the Old Testament (e.g. 2 Samuel 12:30) refers to physical mass rather than coined currency. The bronze for the Tabernacle (Exodus 38:29) was 70 talents and 2,400 shekels.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַמּוֹן (Ammon) - בְּנֵי עַמּוֹן (bene Ammon), sons of Ammon
translationNotes.note: A kingdom east of the Jordan around Rabbah, modern Amman, descended from Lot through his younger daughter (Genesis 19:38). Their national god was Milcom, also called Molech, whose worship took children in fire. Israel was told not to harass them on the way to Canaan (Deuteronomy 2:19), but the border wars run from Judges 11 to Nehemiah 4.

Hanun shaves David's envoys and cuts their robes off at the hip (verse 4). Both halves are calculated insults: an adult man's beard marked his standing, and cutting the garment at the buttocks exposed him the way prisoners of war were stripped and paraded (Isaiah 20:4). Diplomatic envoys were protected persons, so this was an act of war, not rudeness.

stories.keyTakeaway: Hanun shaves and humiliates David’s envoys, and the Ammonites hire Aramean chariots and troops; Joab and Abishai put them to flight, and when the Arameans regroup under Shophach, David himself crosses the Jordan, defeats them, kills Shophach, and Hadadezer’s subjects make peace with Israel.

stories.title: ⚔️ 1 Chronicles 20
summaryBullets: In the spring, at the time when kings march out to war, Joab led out the army and ravaged the land of the Ammonites. He came to Rabbah and besieged it, but David remained in Jerusalem. And Joab attacked Rabbah and demolished it. (20:1).

Then David took the crown from the head of their king. It was found to weigh a talent of gold and was set with precious stones, and it was placed on David’s head. And David took a great amount of plunder from the city. (20:2).

David brought out the people who were there and put them to work with saws, iron picks, and axes. And he did the same to all the Ammonite cities. Then David and all his troops returned to Jerusalem. (20:3).
Some time later, war broke out with the Philistines at Gezer. At that time Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Sippai, a descendant of the Rephaim, and the Philistines were subdued. (20:4).
Once again there was a battle with the Philistines, and Elhanan son of Jair killed Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver’s beam. (20:5).
And there was also a battle at Gath, where there was a man of great stature with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot— twenty-four in all. He too was descended from Rapha, (20:6).
and when he taunted Israel, Jonathan the son of David’s brother Shimei killed him. (20:7).
So these descendants of Rapha in Gath fell at the hands of David and his servants. (20:8).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 11:1: In the spring, when kings go out to battle, David sent Joab and stayed in Jerusalem.
2 Samuel 12:26-31: The same fall of Rabbah, the crown of a talent of gold, and the forced labour.
1 Samuel 17:4-7: Goliath of Gath, six cubits and a span tall, with a spear shaft like a weaver's beam.
2 Samuel 21:15-22: The parallel roll of four Philistine giants killed by David's men.
Numbers 13:32-33: The spies report men of great size in the land, the descendants of Anak.

translationNotes.note: The largest unit of weight and money in the ancient world. A talent of silver weighed about 75 lbs (34 kg) and equaled roughly 6,000 denarii; about 20 years of a laborer's wages. A talent of gold was worth far more. When Jesus tells the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30), each talent represents a staggering trust.

The Ammonite capital, about twenty-three miles east of the Jordan on the King's Highway trade route; the site is modern Amman. It sat on a high citadel above a spring, which is why a siege rather than an assault was needed and why taking the water supply broke it (2 Samuel 12:27). Verse 1 has Joab do the work while David stays home.

Verses 4, 6, and 8 call Sippai, Lahmi, and the six-fingered man at Gath descendants of the Rapha. Israel had met unusually large men before: the spies reported them at Numbers 13:32-33, and Og king of Bashan slept in an iron bed thirteen and a half feet long (Deuteronomy 3:11). They survived in the Philistine cities of the coast after Joshua cleared them from the hill country (Joshua 11:22).

The crown in verse 2 weighs a talent, about 75 pounds. No head wears that, so it was lifted from the idol or the throne and held above David rather than worn; the text says its weight was found to be a talent and that a precious stone from it went into David's crown. As bullion that is a fortune: gold at any period is priced by the ounce, and a talent is about 1,200 troy ounces.

stories.keyTakeaway: Joab besieges and destroys Rabbah while David remains in Jerusalem, takes the Ammonite king's crown and plunder, and puts the conquered people to forced labor. David's forces then fight several battles against the Philistines, with his men killing several giants including Lahmi the brother of Goliath.

stories.title: ⚔️ 1 Chronicles 21
summaryBullets: Then Satan rose up against Israel and incited David to take a census of Israel. (21:1).
So David said to Joab and the commanders of the troops, “Go and count the Israelites from Beersheba to Dan and bring me a report, so that I may know their number.” (21:2).

But Joab replied, “May the LORD multiply His troops a hundred times over. My lord the king, are they not all servants of my lord? Why does my lord want to do this? Why should he bring guilt on Israel?” (21:3).
Nevertheless , the king’s word prevailed against Joab. So Joab departed and traveled throughout Israel, and then he returned to Jerusalem. (21:4).
And Joab reported to David the total number of the troops. In all Israel there were 1,100,000 men who drew the sword, including 470,000 in Judah. (21:5).
But Joab did not include Levi and Benjamin in the count, because the king’s command was detestable to him. (21:6).
This command was also evil in the sight of God; so He struck Israel. (21:7).
Then David said to God, “I have sinned greatly because I have done this thing. Now I beg You to take away the iniquity of Your servant, for I have acted very foolishly.” (21:8).
And the LORD instructed Gad, David’s seer, (21:9).
“Go and tell David that this is what the LORD says: ‘I am offering you three options. Choose one of them, and I will carry it out against you.’” (21:10).
So Gad went and said to David, “This is what the LORD says: ‘You must choose (21:11).

between three years of famine, three months of being swept away before your enemies and overtaken by their swords, or three days of the sword of the LORD— days of plague upon the land, with the angel of the LORD ravaging every part of Israel.’ Now then, decide how I should reply to Him who sent me.” (21:12).
David answered Gad, “I am deeply distressed. Please, let me fall into the hand of the LORD, for His mercies are very great; but do not let me fall into the hands of men.” (21:13).
So the LORD sent a plague upon Israel, and seventy thousand men of Israel fell dead. (21:14).

Then God sent an angel to destroy Jerusalem, but as the angel was doing so, the LORD saw it and relented from the calamity, and He said to the angel who was destroying the people, “Enough! Withdraw your hand now!” At that time the angel of the LORD was standing by the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. (21:15).

When David lifted up his eyes and saw the angel of the LORD standing between heaven and earth, with a drawn sword in his hand stretched out over Jerusalem, David and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell facedown. (21:16).

And David said to God, “Was it not I who gave the order to count the people? I am the one who has sinned and acted wickedly. But these sheep, what have they done? O LORD my God, please let Your hand fall upon me and my father’s house, but do not let this plague remain upon Your people.” (21:17).
Then the angel of the LORD ordered Gad to tell David to go up and build an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. (21:18).
So David went up at the word that Gad had spoken in the name of the LORD. (21:19).
Now Ornan was threshing wheat when he turned and saw the angel; and his four sons who were with him hid themselves. (21:20).
David came to Ornan, and when Ornan looked out and saw David, he left the threshing floor and bowed facedown before David. (21:21).

Then David said to Ornan, “Grant me the site of this threshing floor, that I may build an altar to the LORD. Sell it to me for the full price, so that the plague upon the people may be halted.” (21:22).

Ornan said to David, “Take it! May my lord the king do whatever seems good to him. Look, I will give the oxen for the burnt offerings, the threshing sledges for the wood, and the wheat for the grain offering— I will give it all.” (21:23).
“No,” replied King David, “I insist on paying the full price, for I will not take for the LORD what belongs to you, nor will I offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing.” (21:24).
So David paid Ornan six hundred shekels of gold for the site. (21:25).
And there he built an altar to the LORD and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. He called upon the LORD, who answered him with fire from heaven on the altar of burnt offering. (21:26).
Then the LORD spoke to the angel, who put his sword back into its sheath. (21:27).
At that time, when David saw that the LORD had answered him at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, he offered sacrifices there. (21:28).
For the tabernacle of the LORD that Moses had made in the wilderness and the altar of burnt offering were presently at the high place in Gibeon, (21:29).
but David could not go before it to inquire of God, because he was afraid of the sword of the angel of the LORD. (21:30).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 24:1-25: The same census, the same three-day plague, and the purchase of Araunah's threshing floor.
Exodus 30:11-16: Every man counted in a census must pay a half shekel ransom so that no plague breaks out.
2 Chronicles 3:1: Solomon builds the temple on Mount Moriah, at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.
Genesis 22:2,14: Abraham is sent to the land of Moriah, and names the place The LORD Will Provide.
Job 1:6-12: Satan presents himself before the LORD and is given leave to strike everything Job has.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָּׂטָן (śatan), Greek: διάβολος (diabolos), Aramaic: שטנא (satana)
translationNotes.note: Means 'adversary/opponent.' In this context, a personal adversary or the Accuser; 2 Samuel 24 attributes incitement to God directly, showing theological tension.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִפְקָד (mifqad), Greek: ἀριθμός (arithmos), Aramaic: מנינא (menina)
translationNotes.note: Counting people as an assertion of control; viewed as prideful and lacking trust in God’s provision.

A flat, hard, outdoor surface, usually a leveled rock or beaten-earth circle at the edge of town, where harvested grain was separated from chaff. Oxen pulled a wooden sledge over the stalks; the mixed kernels and chaff were then winnowed in the wind. Threshing floors doubled as public civic spaces (Ruth 3; 2 Samuel 24:18; Solomon's temple site).

A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

A shekel is a weight, not a coin, about 0.4 ounces or 11.4 grams. Six hundred shekels of gold is roughly fifteen pounds of gold, paid in verse 25 for the site. The parallel at 2 Samuel 24:24 records fifty shekels of silver for the floor itself and the oxen; Chronicles gives the price of the whole place.

The same man is Ornan here and Araunah in 2 Samuel 24. He is a Jebusite, one of the original inhabitants of Jerusalem still living and farming there after David took the city, which is why he owns a working threshing floor on the ridge north of it. That ridge is where the temple goes up (2 Chronicles 3:1).

stories.keyTakeaway: Satan rises against Israel and incites David to count the fighting men; the LORD sends a plague that kills seventy thousand, then halts the destroying angel at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, where David buys the site, builds an altar, and offers sacrifices, and the LORD answers with fire from heaven.

stories.title: 🪚 1 Chronicles 22
summaryBullets: Then David said, “Here shall be the house of the LORD God, as well as the altar of burnt offering for Israel.” (22:1).
So David gave orders to gather the foreigners in the land of Israel, from whom he appointed stonecutters to prepare finished stones for building the house of God. (22:2).
David provided a large quantity of iron to make the nails for the doors of the gateways and for the fittings, together with more bronze than could be weighed (22:3).
and more cedar logs than could be counted; for the Sidonians and Tyrians had brought a large quantity of cedar logs to David. (22:4).

And David said, “My son Solomon is young and inexperienced, and the house to be built for the LORD must be exceedingly magnificent — famous and glorious throughout all lands. Therefore I must make preparations for it.” So David made lavish preparations before his death. (22:5).
Then David called for his son Solomon and instructed him to build a house for the LORD, the God of Israel. (22:6).
“My son,” said David to Solomon, “it was in my heart to build a house for the Name of the LORD my God, (22:7).
but this word of the LORD came to me: ‘You have shed much blood and waged great wars. You are not to build a house for My Name because you have shed so much blood on the ground before Me. (22:8).

But a son will be born to you who will be a man of rest. I will give him rest from all his enemies on every side; for his name will be Solomon, and I will grant to Israel peace and quiet during his reign. (22:9).
He is the one who will build a house for My Name. He will be My son, and I will be his Father. And I will establish the throne of his kingdom over Israel forever.’ (22:10).
Now, my son, may the LORD be with you, and may you succeed in building the house of the LORD your God, as He said you would. (22:11).
Above all, may the LORD give you insight and understanding when He puts you in command over Israel, so that you may keep the Law of the LORD your God. (22:12).
Then you will succeed, if you carefully follow the statutes and ordinances that the LORD commanded Moses for Israel. Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid or discouraged. (22:13).

Now behold, I have taken great pains to provide for the house of the LORD— 100,000 talents of gold, 1,000,000 talents of silver, and bronze and iron too great to be weighed. I have also provided timber and stone, and you may add to them. (22:14).
You also have many workers: stonecutters, masons, carpenters, and men skilled in every kind of work — (22:15).
in gold and silver, bronze and iron— craftsmen beyond number. Now begin the work, and may the LORD be with you.” (22:16).
Then David ordered all the leaders of Israel to help his son Solomon: (22:17).

“Is not the LORD your God with you, and has He not granted you rest on every side? For He has given the inhabitants of the land into my hand, and the land has been subdued before the LORD and His people. (22:18).

Now set your heart and soul to seek the LORD your God. Begin building the sanctuary of the LORD God, so that you may bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD and the holy articles of God into the temple that will be built for the Name of the LORD.” (22:19).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 7:12-13: God promises David’s son will build the house.
1 Kings 5:3-5: Solomon recounts why David could not build the temple.
Deuteronomy 12:10-11: A place of rest and God’s chosen dwelling.
Isaiah 9:6: Messiah called 'Prince of Peace,' like Solomon’s role in contrast to David.

The largest unit of weight and money in the ancient world. A talent of silver weighed about 75 lbs (34 kg) and equaled roughly 6,000 denarii; about 20 years of a laborer's wages. A talent of gold was worth far more. When Jesus tells the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30), each talent represents a staggering trust.

About 75 lbs (34 kg) of metal. A 'talent of gold' in the Old Testament (e.g. 2 Samuel 12:30) refers to physical mass rather than coined currency. The bronze for the Tabernacle (Exodus 38:29) was 70 talents and 2,400 shekels.
