stories.title: 👑 1 Chronicles 23
summaryBullets: When David was old and full of years, he installed his son Solomon as king over Israel. (23:1).
Then he gathered all the leaders of Israel, as well as the priests and Levites. (23:2).
The Levites thirty years of age or older were counted, and the total number of men was 38,000. (23:3).
“Of these,” said David, “24,000 are to oversee the work of the house of the LORD, 6,000 are to be officers and judges, (23:4).
4,000 are to be gatekeepers, and 4,000 are to praise the LORD with the instruments I have made for giving praise.” (23:5).
Then David divided the Levites into divisions according to the sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. (23:6).
The Gershonites: Ladan and Shimei. (23:7).
The sons of Ladan: Jehiel the first, Zetham, and Joel— three in all. (23:8).
The sons of Shimei: Shelomoth, Haziel, and Haran— three in all. These were the heads of the families of Ladan. (23:9).
And the sons of Shimei: Jahath, Zina, Jeush, and Beriah. These were the sons of Shimei— four in all. (23:10).
Jahath was the first and Zizah was the second; but Jeush and Beriah did not have many sons, so they were counted as one family and received a single assignment. (23:11).
The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel— four in all. (23:12).

The sons of Amram: Aaron and Moses. Aaron and his descendants were set apart forever to consecrate the most holy things, to burn incense before the LORD, to minister before Him, and to pronounce blessings in His name forever. (23:13).
As for Moses the man of God, his sons were named among the tribe of Levi. (23:14).
The sons of Moses: Gershom and Eliezer. (23:15).
The descendants of Gershom: Shebuel was the first. (23:16).
The descendants of Eliezer: Rehabiah was the first. Eliezer did not have any other sons, but the sons of Rehabiah were very numerous. (23:17).
The sons of Izhar: Shelomith was the first. (23:18).
The sons of Hebron: Jeriah was the first, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth. (23:19).
The sons of Uzziel: Micah was the first and Isshiah the second. (23:20).
The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. The sons of Mahli: Eleazar and Kish. (23:21).
Eleazar died without having any sons; he had only daughters. Their cousins, the sons of Kish, married them. (23:22).
The sons of Mushi: Mahli, Eder, and Jeremoth— three in all. (23:23).

These were the descendants of Levi by their families— the heads of families, registered individually by name— those twenty years of age or older who worked in the service of the house of the LORD. (23:24).
For David had said, “The LORD, the God of Israel, has given rest to His people and has come to dwell in Jerusalem forever. (23:25).
So now the Levites no longer need to carry the tabernacle or any of the articles for its service.” (23:26).
For according to the final instructions of David, the Levites twenty years of age or older were counted, (23:27).

but their duty was to assist the descendants of Aaron with the service of the house of the LORD, being responsible for the courts and chambers, the purification of all the holy things, and the work of the service of the house of God, (23:28).
as well as for the rows of the showbread, the fine flour for the grain offering, the wafers of unleavened bread, the baking, the mixing, and all measurements of quantity and size. (23:29).
They were also to stand every morning to give thanks and praise to the LORD, and likewise in the evening. (23:30).
Whenever burnt offerings were presented to the LORD on the Sabbaths, New Moons, and appointed feasts, they were to serve regularly before the LORD in the numbers prescribed for them. (23:31).
So the Levites were to carry out the responsibilities for the Tent of Meeting and the Holy Place, and, under their brothers the descendants of Aaron, the service of the house of the LORD. (23:32).
crossRefs: Numbers 4:1-3: Levites are counted from thirty years old to fifty for the service of the tent of meeting.
Numbers 8:23-26: Levites begin service at twenty-five and retire from the heavy work at fifty.
Numbers 3:5-10: The Levites are given to Aaron and his sons to do the work of the tabernacle.
Deuteronomy 10:8-9: Levi carries the ark, stands to minister, and blesses in the LORD's name, with no land inheritance.
Exodus 6:16-19: The sons of Levi by their generations: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.

translationNotes.note: The tribe of Levi received no territory. Numbers 18:20-24 gives them the tithe instead of land and says the LORD is their portion, and Joshua 21 scatters them through forty-eight towns inside the other tribes. That is why the tribe is organised here by job rather than by border, and why the whole tribe depended on the sanctuary working.

Verse 6 divides the Levites by Levi's three sons, and in the wilderness each clan carried a different part of the tabernacle. Kohath took the ark and the holy vessels on their shoulders with poles, never on a cart (Numbers 4:4-15, 7:9). Gershon took the curtains, coverings, and hangings; Merari took the frames, bars, pillars, and sockets (Numbers 3:25-37, 4:24-33). The divisions here are the same families with the carrying stopped.

Verses 3-5 break the count down: 24,000 over the work of the house, 6,000 officers and judges, 4,000 gatekeepers, and 4,000 musicians. Only a fraction served at any one time, since the men rotated through courses. The rest lived in the Levitical towns and farmed the pastureland attached to them.

Six thousand Levites in verse 4 are set to be officers and judges, which is a civil appointment, not a sanctuary one. Deuteronomy 17:8-9 sends hard cases to the Levitical priests and the judge in office, and 2 Chronicles 19:8-11 has Jehoshaphat station Levites, priests, and heads of families in Jerusalem as a court. The tribe with no land held the courts.

Verse 3 counts Levites from thirty up, then verses 24 and 27 lower it to twenty. The law had already moved the age once, from thirty in Numbers 4:3 to twenty-five in Numbers 8:24. Verse 26 gives the reason for the change: with the tabernacle no longer carried from place to place, the job stopped being heavy lifting and started being permanent temple duty.

stories.keyTakeaway: David appoints Solomon as king and organizes thirty-eight thousand Levites into divisions for temple service, assigning them to maintain the building, lead worship, serve as judges and gatekeepers, and assist Aaron's descendants in handling sacred objects and offerings.

stories.title: 👑 1 Chronicles 24
summaryBullets: These were the divisions of the descendants of Aaron. The sons of Aaron were Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. (24:1).
But Nadab and Abihu died before their father did, and they had no sons; so Eleazar and Ithamar served as priests. (24:2).
With the help of Eleazar’s descendant Zadok and Ithamar’s descendant Ahimelech, David divided them according to the offices of their service. (24:3).

Since more leaders were found among Eleazar’s descendants than those of Ithamar, they were divided accordingly. There were sixteen heads of families from the descendants of Eleazar and eight from the descendants of Ithamar. (24:4).
Thus they were divided by lot, for there were officers of the sanctuary and officers of God among both Eleazar’s and Ithamar’s descendants. (24:5).

The scribe, Shemaiah son of Nethanel, a Levite, recorded their names in the presence of the king and of the officers: Zadok the priest, Ahimelech son of Abiathar, and the heads of families of the priests and the Levites — one family being taken from Eleazar, and then one from Ithamar. (24:6).
The first lot fell to Jehoiarib, the second to Jedaiah, (24:7).
the third to Harim, the fourth to Seorim, (24:8).
the fifth to Malchijah, the sixth to Mijamin, (24:9).
the seventh to Hakkoz, the eighth to Abijah, (24:10).
the ninth to Jeshua, the tenth to Shecaniah, (24:11).
the eleventh to Eliashib, the twelfth to Jakim, (24:12).
the thirteenth to Huppah, the fourteenth to Jeshebeab, (24:13).
the fifteenth to Bilgah, the sixteenth to Immer, (24:14).
the seventeenth to Hezir, the eighteenth to Happizzez, (24:15).
the nineteenth to Pethahiah, the twentieth to Jehezkel, (24:16).
the twenty-first to Jachin, the twenty-second to Gamul, (24:17).
the twenty-third to Delaiah, and the twenty-fourth to Maaziah. (24:18).

This was their appointed order for service when they entered the house of the LORD, according to the regulations prescribed for them by their forefather Aaron, as the LORD, the God of Israel, had commanded him. (24:19).
Now these were the rest of the descendants of Levi: From the sons of Amram: Shubael; from the sons of Shubael: Jehdeiah. (24:20).
As for Rehabiah, from his sons: The first was Isshiah. (24:21).
From the Izharites: Shelomoth; from the sons of Shelomoth: Jahath. (24:22).
From the sons of Hebron: Jeriah was the first, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth. (24:23).
From the sons of Uzziel: Micah; from the sons of Micah: Shamir. (24:24).
The brother of Micah: Isshiah; from the sons of Isshiah: Zechariah. (24:25).
The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. The son of Jaaziah: Beno. (24:26).
The descendants of Merari from Jaaziah: Beno, Shoham, Zaccur, and Ibri. (24:27).
From Mahli: Eleazar, who had no sons. (24:28).
From Kish: Jerahmeel the son of Kish. (24:29).
And the sons of Mushi: Mahli, Eder, and Jerimoth. These were the sons of the Levites, according to their families. (24:30).

As their brothers the descendants of Aaron did, they also cast lots in the presence of King David and of Zadok, Ahimelech, and the heads of the families of the priests and Levites— the family heads and their younger brothers alike. (24:31).
crossRefs: Leviticus 10:1-7: Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire before the LORD and are killed by it.
Numbers 3:2-4: Aaron's four sons are named, and Eleazar and Ithamar serve as priests after the other two die.
Luke 1:5-9: Zechariah belongs to the division of Abijah, and the lot falls to him to burn incense.
1 Samuel 2:30-36: The word against Eli's house, and the promise to raise up a faithful priest.
Proverbs 16:33: The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.

translationNotes.note: Verse 2 says Aaron's two eldest sons 'died before their father did, and they had no sons.' Leviticus 10:1-2 records why: they offered unauthorised fire before the LORD and fire came out and consumed them. Because they left no sons, the entire priesthood of Israel descends from the two younger brothers, which is what the rest of this chapter divides up.

The two surviving priestly houses. Verse 4 counts sixteen heads of families from Eleazar and eight from Ithamar, and verse 3 names their leading men in David's day: Zadok from Eleazar's side, Ahimelech from Ithamar's. Verse 5 divides the offices by lot between the two houses so neither could claim precedence by numbers.

Too many priests existed to serve at once, so David sorted them into twenty-four courses that rotated through the sanctuary about a week each, twice a year, plus all hands at the three pilgrim feasts. The order was fixed by lot and stayed fixed for a thousand years: Luke 1:5 still places Zechariah in the eighth course, Abijah, which is verse 10 of this chapter.

Marked stones or sticks were shaken or drawn to settle a decision, and Israel treated the outcome as God's answer rather than chance (Proverbs 16:33). It was used to divide the land (Joshua 18:6), to find Achan (Joshua 7:14), and here to set the priestly order so no family could claim precedence. The apostles use it once more in Acts 1:26.

stories.keyTakeaway: David divides Aaron's descendants into twenty-four divisions for priestly service, with lots cast impartially between Eleazar's and Ithamar's lines; he also organizes the remaining Levites into family groups by casting lots.

stories.title: 👑 1 Chronicles 25
summaryBullets: Additionally, David and the commanders of the army set apart some of the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun to prophesy with the accompaniment of lyres, harps, and cymbals. The following is the list of the men who performed this service: (25:1).
From the sons of Asaph: Zaccur, Joseph, Nethaniah, and Asarelah. These sons of Asaph were under the direction of Asaph, who prophesied under the direction of the king. (25:2).

From the sons of Jeduthun: Gedaliah, Zeri, Jeshaiah , Shimei, Hashabiah, and Mattithiah — six in all — under the direction of their father Jeduthun, who prophesied with the harp, giving thanks and praise to the LORD. (25:3).
From the sons of Heman: Bukkiah, Mattaniah, Uzziel, Shebuel, Jerimoth, Hananiah, Hanani, Eliathah, Giddalti, Romamti-ezer, Joshbekashah, Mallothi, Hothir, and Mahazioth. (25:4).
All these sons of Heman the king’s seer were given him through the promises of God to exalt him, for God had given Heman fourteen sons and three daughters. (25:5).

All these were under the direction of their fathers for the music of the house of the LORD with cymbals, harps, and lyres, for the service of the house of God. Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman were under the direction of the king. (25:6).
Together with their relatives, who were all trained and skillful in the songs of the LORD, they numbered 288. (25:7).
They cast lots for their duties, young and old alike, teacher as well as pupil. (25:8).
The first lot, which was for Asaph, fell to Joseph, his sons, and his brothers—12 in all; the second to Gedaliah, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:9).
the third to Zaccur, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:10).
the fourth to Izri, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:11).
the fifth to Nethaniah, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:12).
the sixth to Bukkiah, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:13).
the seventh to Jesarelah, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:14).
the eighth to Jeshaiah, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:15).
the ninth to Mattaniah, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:16).
the tenth to Shimei, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:17).
the eleventh to Azarel, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:18).
the twelfth to Hashabiah, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:19).
the thirteenth to Shubael, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:20).
the fourteenth to Mattithiah, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:21).
the fifteenth to Jeremoth, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:22).
the sixteenth to Hananiah, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:23).
the seventeenth to Joshbekashah, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:24).
the eighteenth to Hanani, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:25).
the nineteenth to Mallothi, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:26).
the twentieth to Eliathah, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:27).
the twenty-first to Hothir, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:28).
the twenty-second to Giddalti, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:29).
the twenty-third to Mahazioth, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all; (25:30).
and the twenty-fourth to Romamti-ezer, his sons, and his brothers— 12 in all. (25:31).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 10:5-6: A band of prophets comes down from the high place with harp, tambourine, flute, and lyre, prophesying.
2 Kings 3:15: Elisha calls for a musician, and while the man plays the hand of the LORD comes on him.
1 Chronicles 16:4-7: Asaph is first appointed before the ark to invoke, thank, and praise the LORD.
2 Chronicles 29:25-30: Hezekiah stations Levites with cymbals, harps, and lyres by the command of David and the prophets.
Psalm 73:1-28: One of the twelve psalms carried under Asaph's name, whose sons are set apart here.

translationNotes.note: Verses 1 to 3 describe men set apart to prophesy with lyres, harps, and cymbals. The Hebrew uses the ordinary word for prophesying, so the temple singing was not treated as background music but as declaring God's word aloud in ordered form. The same link between music and prophecy shows up at 1 Samuel 10:5 and 2 Kings 3:15.

The kinnor was a small hand-held lyre, light enough to carry and play walking, and is the instrument David played for Saul. The nevel was a larger stringed instrument with a fuller sound. The metsiltayim were bronze cymbals, named as a pair, used to mark the beat rather than to carry a tune.

Verse 5 calls Heman 'the king's seer.' A hozeh held a standing post in the royal household, distinct from a prophet who appeared unbidden. Gad is called David's seer at 2 Samuel 24:11, and 2 Chronicles 35:15 lists Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun together as the king's seers. Heman ran the music and held a court office at the same time.

Verse 7 numbers the trained singers at 288, and verse 9 onward divides them into twenty-four lots. That is exactly twelve men to a course, matched one for one against the twenty-four courses of priests in the previous chapter, so a full shift of singers went on duty with every shift of priests.

The last sons of Heman in verse 4 carry names that are ordinary Hebrew words rather than usual personal names. Giddalti means 'I have magnified,' Mallothi 'I have uttered,' Hothir 'he gave in abundance,' Mahazioth 'visions,' and Romamti-ezer 'I have exalted help.' The English transliteration hides all of it.

stories.keyTakeaway: David and the commanders set apart sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun for prophesying and music in the temple; 288 trained musicians cast lots to determine their twenty-four rotating service assignments.

stories.title: 👑 1 Chronicles 26
summaryBullets: These were the divisions of the gatekeepers: From the Korahites: Meshelemiah son of Kore, one of the sons of Asaph. (26:1).
Meshelemiah had sons: Zechariah the firstborn, Jediael the second, Zebadiah the third, Jathniel the fourth, (26:2).
Elam the fifth, Jehohanan the sixth, and Eliehoenai the seventh. (26:3).
And Obed-edom also had sons: Shemaiah the firstborn, Jehozabad the second, Joah the third, Sachar the fourth, Nethanel the fifth, (26:4).
Ammiel the sixth, Issachar the seventh, and Peullethai the eighth. For God had blessed Obed-edom. (26:5).
Also to his son Shemaiah were born sons who ruled over their families because they were strong, capable men. (26:6).
Shemaiah’s sons were Othni, Rephael, Obed, and Elzabad; his brothers were Elihu and Semachiah, also capable men. (26:7).
All these were descendants of Obed-edom; they and their sons and brothers were capable men with strength to do the work— 62 in all from Obed-edom. (26:8).
Meshelemiah also had sons and brothers who were capable men— 18 in all. (26:9).
Hosah the Merarite also had sons: Shimri the first (although he was not the firstborn, his father had appointed him as the first), (26:10).
Hilkiah the second, Tebaliah the third, and Zechariah the fourth. The sons and brothers of Hosah numbered 13 in all. (26:11).
These divisions of the gatekeepers, through their chief men, had duties for ministering in the house of the LORD, just as their relatives did. (26:12).
They cast lots for each gate, according to their families, young and old alike. (26:13).
The lot for the East Gate fell to Shelemiah. Then lots were cast for his son Zechariah, a wise counselor, and the lot for the North Gate fell to him. (26:14).
The lot for the South Gate fell to Obed-edom, and the lot for the storehouses to his sons. (26:15).
The lots for the West Gate and the Shallecheth Gate on the ascending highway fell to Shuppim and Hosah. There were guards stationed at every watch. (26:16).
Each day there were six Levites on the east, four on the north, four on the south, and two pairs at the storehouse. (26:17).
As for the court on the west, there were four at the highway and two at the court. (26:18).
These were the divisions of the gatekeepers who were descendants of Korah and Merari. (26:19).
Now their fellow Levites were in charge of the treasuries of the house of God and the treasuries of the dedicated things. (26:20).
From the descendants of Ladan, who were Gershonites through Ladan and heads of the families of Ladan the Gershonite, were Jehieli, (26:21).
the sons of Jehieli, Zetham, and his brother Joel. They were in charge of the treasuries of the house of the LORD. (26:22).
From the Amramites, the Izharites, the Hebronites, and the Uzzielites: (26:23).
Shebuel, a descendant of Gershom son of Moses, was the officer in charge of the treasuries. (26:24).
His relatives through Eliezer included Rehabiah his son, Jeshaiah his son, Joram his son, Zichri his son, and Shelomith his son. (26:25).

This Shelomith and his brothers were in charge of all the treasuries for the things dedicated by King David, by the heads of families who were the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and by the army commanders. (26:26).
They had dedicated some of the plunder from their battles to the repair of the house of the LORD. (26:27).

Everything that had been dedicated by Samuel the seer, Saul son of Kish, Abner son of Ner, and Joab son of Zeruiah, along with everything else that was dedicated, was under the care of Shelomith and his brothers. (26:28).
From the Izharites, Chenaniah and his sons had the outside duties as officers and judges over Israel. (26:29).
From the Hebronites, Hashabiah and his relatives, 1,700 capable men, had charge of the affairs of Israel west of the Jordan for all the work of the LORD and for the service of the king. (26:30).

As for the Hebronites, Jerijah was the chief of the Hebronites, according to the genealogies of his ancestors. In the fortieth year of David’s reign the records were searched, and strong, capable men were found among the Hebronites at Jazer in Gilead. (26:31).

Among Jerijah’s relatives there were 2,700 capable men who were heads of families. King David appointed them over the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh for every matter pertaining to God and for the affairs of the king. (26:32).
crossRefs: Numbers 16:1-35: Korah the Levite and his company are swallowed by the earth for seizing the priesthood.
Numbers 26:9-11: The sons of Korah did not die, and their line continued in Israel.
Psalm 84:10: Better one day in Your courts, and to stand at the threshold of God's house, than a thousand elsewhere.
2 Kings 12:9-10: The priest who guards the threshold sets a chest beside the altar for the money brought in.
1 Chronicles 13:13-14: Obed-edom keeps the ark in his house three months, and the LORD blesses his household.

translationNotes.note: Not ushers. These were armed Levites on standing watch at the sanctuary gates and storehouses, twenty-four posts split east, west, north, and south (verses 17-18), controlling who and what came in. They also held the keys, opened at dawn, and guarded the treasuries of dedicated gifts described in verses 20-28.

Verses 4-8 count sixty-two men of his house among the gatekeepers. This is the man the ark was left with for three months after Uzza died, and 1 Chronicles 13:14 says the LORD blessed his household during that time, which is what moved David to try the move again. His family ends up on permanent duty at the doors.

Verses 26-28 describe a separate treasury funded from war plunder, dedicated by Samuel the seer, by Saul, by Abner, by Joab, and by the army commanders, and set aside for the repair of the house of the LORD. Captured metal and goods were signed over to the sanctuary rather than divided, and Levites kept the account of it.

translationNotes.term: Officers over the affairs of Israel
translationNotes.note: Verses 29-32 put Levites outside the temple altogether: Chenaniah and his sons on 'the outside duties as officers and judges,' 1,700 men over Israel west of the Jordan, and 2,700 over Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh east of it, 'for every matter pertaining to God and for the affairs of the king.' One body of men handled both religious and royal business in the provinces.

stories.keyTakeaway: The temple gatekeepers and Levites are organized by family divisions and assigned to different gates and duties; other Levites are appointed to manage the temple treasuries, serve as officials and judges, and oversee the work of the Lord and the king's service.

stories.title: 👑 1 Chronicles 27
summaryBullets: This is the list of the Israelites— the heads of families, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and their officers who served the king in every matter concerning the divisions on rotating military duty each month throughout the year. There were 24,000 men in each division: (27:1).
Jashobeam son of Zabdiel was in charge of the first division, which was assigned the first month. There were 24,000 men in his division. (27:2).
He was a descendant of Perez and chief of all the army commanders for the first month. (27:3).
Dodai the Ahohite was in charge of the division for the second month, and Mikloth was the leader. There were 24,000 men in his division. (27:4).
The third army commander, as chief for the third month, was Benaiah son of Jehoiada the priest. There were 24,000 men in his division. (27:5).
This Benaiah was mighty among the Thirty and was over the Thirty, and his son Ammizabad was in charge of his division. (27:6).
The fourth, for the fourth month, was Joab’s brother Asahel, and his son Zebadiah was commander after him. There were 24,000 men in his division. (27:7).
The fifth, for the fifth month, was the commander Shamhuth the Izrahite. There were 24,000 men in his division. (27:8).
The sixth, for the sixth month, was Ira son of Ikkesh the Tekoite. There were 24,000 men in his division. (27:9).
The seventh, for the seventh month, was Helez the Pelonite, an Ephraimite. There were 24,000 men in his division. (27:10).
The eighth, for the eighth month, was Sibbecai the Hushathite, a Zerahite. There were 24,000 men in his division. (27:11).
The ninth, for the ninth month, was Abiezer the Anathothite, a Benjamite. There were 24,000 men in his division. (27:12).
The tenth, for the tenth month, was Maharai the Netophathite, a Zerahite. There were 24,000 men in his division. (27:13).
The eleventh, for the eleventh month, was Benaiah the Pirathonite, an Ephraimite. There were 24,000 men in his division. (27:14).
The twelfth, for the twelfth month, was Heldai the Netophathite, from the family of Othniel. There were 24,000 men in his division. (27:15).
These officers were in charge of the tribes of Israel: Over the Reubenites was Eliezer son of Zichri; over the Simeonites was Shephatiah son of Maacah; (27:16).
over Levi was Hashabiah son of Kemuel; over Aaron was Zadok; (27:17).
over Judah was Elihu, one of David’s brothers; over Issachar was Omri son of Michael; (27:18).
over Zebulun was Ishmaiah son of Obadiah; over Naphtali was Jerimoth son of Azriel; (27:19).
over the Ephraimites was Hoshea son of Azaziah; over one of the half-tribes of Manasseh was Joel son of Pedaiah; (27:20).
over the half-tribe of Manasseh in Gilead was Iddo son of Zechariah; over Benjamin was Jaasiel son of Abner; (27:21).
and over Dan was Azarel son of Jeroham. These were the leaders of the tribes of Israel. (27:22).
David did not count the men aged twenty or under, because the LORD had said that He would make Israel as numerous as the stars of the sky. (27:23).
Joab son of Zeruiah began to count the men but did not finish. For because of this census wrath came upon Israel, and the number was not entered in the Book of the Chronicles of King David. (27:24).
Azmaveth son of Adiel was in charge of the royal storehouses. Jonathan son of Uzziah was in charge of the storehouses in the country, in the cities, in the villages, and in the fortresses. (27:25).
Ezri son of Chelub was in charge of the workers in the fields who tilled the soil. (27:26).
Shimei the Ramathite was in charge of the vineyards. Zabdi the Shiphmite was in charge of the produce of the vineyards for the wine vats. (27:27).
Baal-hanan the Gederite was in charge of the olive and sycamore trees in the foothills. Joash was in charge of the stores of olive oil. (27:28).
Shitrai the Sharonite was in charge of the herds grazing in Sharon. Shaphat son of Adlai was in charge of the herds in the valleys. (27:29).
Obil the Ishmaelite was in charge of the camels. Jehdeiah the Meronothite was in charge of the donkeys. (27:30).
Jaziz the Hagrite was in charge of the flocks. All these officials were in charge of King David’s property. (27:31).
David’s uncle Jonathan was a counselor; he was a man of insight and a scribe. Jehiel son of Hachmoni attended to the sons of the king. (27:32).
Ahithophel was the king’s counselor. Hushai the Archite was the king’s friend. (27:33).
Ahithophel was succeeded by Jehoiada son of Benaiah, then by Abiathar. Joab was the commander of the king’s army. (27:34).
crossRefs: 1 Chronicles 21:1-7: Joab begins the census under protest and never counts Levi or Benjamin.
2 Samuel 15:31-37: Ahithophel joins Absalom, and Hushai the Archite is sent back to defeat his counsel.
2 Samuel 17:1-14,23: Ahithophel's advice is set aside, and he goes home, sets his house in order, and hangs himself.
1 Kings 4:7-19: Solomon's twelve officers, each responsible for provisioning the royal household one month a year.
1 Chronicles 11:6-9: Joab is made chief and commander for going up first against the Jebusite stronghold.

translationNotes.note: Twelve divisions of 24,000 men rotating one month each is a militia roster, not a standing army; farmers served their month and went home to the harvest. The Hebrew word rendered thousand, eleph, is also used for a clan or military unit, which is why the totals in Israel's musters read so large. Verse 24 notes the census that produced these numbers was never even finished.

Verses 16-22 name a chief officer for each tribe, but the list runs to thirteen entries and does not match the usual roll. Aaron has an officer of his own, Levi is listed separately, Manasseh appears twice for its two halves, and Gad and Asher are not named at all. The text records the list as it stands without explaining the omissions.

Verses 25-31 are an inventory of crown land, each holding with a named manager: storehouses in the capital and in the fortresses, field labour, vineyards and wine cellars, olive and sycamore groves in the foothills, cattle in Sharon and in the valleys, camels, donkeys, and flocks. Two of the managers are foreigners hired for the specialism, Obil the Ishmaelite over the camels and Jaziz the Hagrite over the flocks.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׁקְמִים (shiqmim), sycamore figs - שְׁפֵלָה (shephelah), lowland
translationNotes.note: The tree in verse 28 is the sycamore fig, not the plane tree the English name suggests. It grows in the warm Shephelah, the belt of low chalk hills between the coastal plain and the Judean ridge, and its fruit had to be pierced or nipped by hand a few days before picking to ripen properly. That is the trade Amos names as his own at Amos 7:14.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רֵעֶה הַמֶּלֶךְ (reeh ha-melekh), friend of the king
translationNotes.note: Verse 33 lists two court offices side by side. The counselor, yoets, advised on policy, and Ahithophel's advice was reckoned in his day as though a man had enquired of God (2 Samuel 16:23). 'The king's friend' was a formal title for the king's closest confidant, held here by Hushai the Archite, and both offices turn on Absalom's revolt in 2 Samuel 15-17.

stories.keyTakeaway: The chapter lists twelve military commanders who each led 24,000 men on rotating monthly duty, followed by the leaders of the twelve tribes and officials overseeing the king's storehouses, farms, herds, and other property. Joab began numbering the men but did not finish, and God's wrath came on Israel because of this census.

headings.text: The Leaders of the Twelve Tribes

stories.title: 👑 1 Chronicles 28
summaryBullets: Now David summoned all the leaders of Israel to Jerusalem: the leaders of the tribes, the leaders of the divisions in the king’s service, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and the officials in charge of all the property and cattle of the king and his sons, along with the court officials and mighty men— every mighty man of valor. (28:1).

Then King David rose to his feet and said, “Listen to me, my brothers and my people. It was in my heart to build a house as a resting place for the ark of the covenant of the LORD and as a footstool for our God. I had made preparations to build it, (28:2).
but God said to me, ‘You are not to build a house for My Name, because you are a man of war who has shed blood.’ (28:3).

Yet the LORD, the God of Israel, chose me out of all my father’s house to be king over Israel forever. For He chose Judah as leader, and from the house of Judah He chose my father’s household, and from my father’s sons He was pleased to make me king over all Israel. (28:4).
And of all my sons— for the LORD has given me many sons— He has chosen Solomon my son to sit on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel. (28:5).
And He said to me, ‘Solomon your son is the one who will build My house and My courts, for I have chosen him as My son, and I will be his Father. (28:6).
I will establish his kingdom forever, if he resolutely carries out My commandments and ordinances, as is being done this day.’ (28:7).

So now in the sight of all Israel, the assembly of the LORD, and in the hearing of our God, keep and seek out all the commandments of the LORD your God, so that you may possess this good land and leave it as an inheritance to your descendants forever. (28:8).

As for you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve Him wholeheartedly and with a willing mind, for the LORD searches every heart and understands the intent of every thought. If you seek Him, He will be found by you; but if you forsake Him, He will reject you forever. (28:9).
Consider now that the LORD has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary. Be strong and do it.” (28:10).
Then David gave his son Solomon the plans for the portico of the temple, its buildings, storehouses, upper rooms, inner rooms, and the room for the mercy seat. (28:11).
The plans contained everything David had in mind for the courts of the house of the LORD, for all the surrounding rooms, for the treasuries of the house of God and of the dedicated things, (28:12).
for the divisions of the priests and Levites, for all the work of service in the house of the LORD, and for all the articles of service in the house of the LORD: (28:13).
the weight of all the gold articles for every kind of service; the weight of all the silver articles for every kind of service; (28:14).

the weight of the gold lampstands and their lamps, including the weight of each lampstand and its lamps; the weight of each silver lampstand and its lamps, according to the use of each lampstand; (28:15).
the weight of gold for each table of showbread, and of silver for the silver tables; (28:16).
the weight of the pure gold for the forks, sprinkling bowls, and pitchers; the weight of each gold dish; the weight of each silver bowl; (28:17).
the weight of the refined gold for the altar of incense; and the plans for the chariot of the gold cherubim that spread their wings and overshadowed the ark of the covenant of the LORD. (28:18).
“All this,” said David, “all the details of this plan, the LORD has made clear to me in writing by His hand upon me.” (28:19).

David also said to Solomon his son, “Be strong and courageous, and do it. Do not be afraid or discouraged, for the LORD God, my God, is with you. He will neither fail you nor forsake you before all the work for the service of the house of the LORD is finished. (28:20).

The divisions of the priests and Levites are ready for all the service of the house of God, and every willing man of every skill will be at your disposal for the work. The officials and all the people are fully at your command.” (28:21).
crossRefs: Exodus 25:9,40: Moses is shown the pattern of the tabernacle and told to make everything according to it.
1 Chronicles 22:6-13: David's earlier private charge to Solomon to build the house and keep the law.
1 Kings 8:17-21: Solomon repeats before the assembly that God chose him, not David, to build the house.
Deuteronomy 31:6-8: Be strong and courageous; the LORD goes with you and will not leave you or forsake you.
Exodus 25:17-22: The mercy seat and the two cherubim of hammered gold above the ark.

translationNotes.note: The word in verses 11, 12, 18, and 19 is the same one used when Moses is shown the tavnit of the tabernacle on the mountain (Exodus 25:9,40). It means a worked model or specification, not a sketch of an idea. Verse 19 says David had it 'in writing from the hand of the LORD,' with the weights of every gold and silver vessel set down.

Verse 1 lists the assembly David summons, and among the tribal leaders and commanders are the sarisim, rendered court officials here and eunuchs elsewhere. The word covers senior household officers of a royal court, men who managed the palace, the harem, and the king's property, and in the surrounding empires such men were commonly castrated so they could hold no dynasty of their own. Potiphar carries the same title at Genesis 37:36.

Verses 14-18 give the plans as a schedule of weights: so much gold for each lampstand and its lamps, so much for each table, for the forks, the bowls, the dishes, the altar of incense. Coined money did not exist in Israel at this period, so gold and silver were reckoned on the scales by shekel and talent. Specifying the weight of each vessel is how a builder specified the vessel.

Verse 18 calls the gold cherubim over the ark a chariot. It is the only place in Scripture the ark's covering figures are named that way, and it fits the descriptions elsewhere of God enthroned above the cherubim (1 Samuel 4:4, Psalm 80:1). The cherubim of Exodus 25:18-20 were beaten from one piece with the mercy seat, facing each other with wings spread over it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֲזַק וֶאֱמָץ (hazaq we-emats), be strong and courageous
translationNotes.note: David's charge to Solomon in verse 20, strong and courageous, do not be afraid, the LORD will not fail you or forsake you, repeats word for word the commission Moses gave Joshua at Deuteronomy 31:6-8 and the LORD gave Joshua at Joshua 1:5-9. The same formula is used again here as one leader hands a national task to his successor.

stories.keyTakeaway: David assembles Israel's leaders and announces that Solomon, not himself, will build the temple because David is a warrior who shed blood; David then hands Solomon detailed architectural plans, specifications for materials, and priestly instructions while charging him to be strong and obey God's commands.

stories.title: 👑 1 Chronicles 29
summaryBullets: Then King David said to the whole assembly, “My son Solomon, the one whom God has chosen, is young and inexperienced. The task is great because this palace is not for man, but for the LORD God. (29:1).

Now with all my ability I have made provision for the house of my God — gold for the gold articles, silver for the silver, bronze for the bronze, iron for the iron, and wood for the wood, as well as onyx for the settings, turquoise, stones of various colors, all kinds of precious stones, and slabs of marble — all in abundance. (29:2).
Moreover, because of my delight in the house of my God, I now give for it my personal treasures of gold and silver, over and above all that I have provided for this holy temple: (29:3).
three thousand talents of gold (the gold of Ophir) and seven thousand talents of refined silver, to overlay the walls of the buildings, (29:4).
for the gold work and the silver work, and for all the work to be done by the craftsmen. Now who is willing to consecrate himself to the LORD today?” (29:5).
Then the leaders of the families, the officers of the tribes of Israel, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and the officials in charge of the king’s work gave willingly. (29:6).
Toward the service of God’s house they gave 5,000 talents and 10,000 darics of gold, 10,000 talents of silver, 18,000 talents of bronze, and 100,000 talents of iron. (29:7).
Whoever had precious stones gave them to the treasury of the house of the LORD, under the care of Jehiel the Gershonite. (29:8).
And the people rejoiced at the willing response of their leaders, for they had given to the LORD freely and wholeheartedly. And King David also rejoiced greatly. (29:9).
Then David blessed the LORD in the sight of all the assembly and said: “May You be blessed, O LORD, God of our father Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. (29:10).

Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the splendor and the majesty, for everything in heaven and on earth belongs to You. Yours, O LORD, is the kingdom, and You are exalted as head over all. (29:11).
Both riches and honor come from You, and You are the ruler over all. In Your hands are power and might to exalt and give strength to all. (29:12).
Now therefore, our God, we give You thanks, and we praise Your glorious name. (29:13).
But who am I, and who are my people, that we should be able to give as generously as this? For everything comes from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You. (29:14).
For we are foreigners and strangers in Your presence, as were all our forefathers. Our days on earth are like a shadow, without hope. (29:15).
O LORD our God, from Your hand comes all this abundance that we have provided to build You a house for Your holy Name, and all of it belongs to You. (29:16).

I know, my God, that You test the heart and delight in uprightness. All these things I have given willingly and with an upright heart, and now I have seen Your people who are present here giving joyfully and willingly to You. (29:17).
O LORD, God of our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, keep this desire forever in the intentions of the hearts of Your people, and direct their hearts toward You. (29:18).
And give my son Solomon a whole heart to keep and carry out all Your commandments, decrees, and statutes, and to build Your palace for which I have made provision.” (29:19).

Then David said to the whole assembly, “Bless the LORD your God.” So the whole assembly blessed the LORD, the God of their fathers. They bowed down and paid homage to the LORD and to the king. (29:20).

The next day they offered sacrifices and presented burnt offerings to the LORD: a thousand bulls, a thousand rams, and a thousand lambs, along with their drink offerings, and other sacrifices in abundance for all Israel. (29:21).

That day they ate and drank with great joy in the presence of the LORD. Then, for a second time, they designated David’s son Solomon as king, anointing him before the LORD as ruler, and Zadok as the priest. (29:22).
So Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD as king in place of his father David. He prospered, and all Israel obeyed him. (29:23).
All the officials and mighty men, as well as all of King David’s sons, pledged their allegiance to King Solomon. (29:24).
The LORD highly exalted Solomon in the sight of all Israel and bestowed on him royal majesty such as had not been bestowed on any king in Israel before him. (29:25).
David son of Jesse was king over all Israel. (29:26).
The length of David’s reign over Israel was forty years — seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem. (29:27).
He died at a ripe old age, full of years, riches, and honor, and his son Solomon reigned in his place. (29:28).
Now the acts of King David, from first to last, are indeed written in the Chronicles of Samuel the Seer, the Chronicles of Nathan the Prophet, and the Chronicles of Gad the Seer, (29:29).
together with all the details of his reign, his might, and the circumstances that came upon him and Israel and all the kingdoms of the lands. (29:30).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 2:10-12: David dies, is buried in the city of David, and Solomon's kingdom is firmly established.
Exodus 35:20-29: Israel brings freewill offerings for the tabernacle until the workmen say there is more than enough.
Ezra 2:68-69: Heads of families give freewill offerings of gold darics and silver minas toward the house of God.
1 Chronicles 22:14-16: David's earlier reckoning of the gold, silver, bronze, and iron laid up for the house.
1 Kings 1:32-40: Solomon's first anointing at Gihon, by Zadok and Nathan, while David still lived.

translationNotes.note: Verses 5-9 turn on this word. A nedavah was given because the giver chose to, over and above every tithe and required sacrifice, and Leviticus 22:21-23 allows a slightly imperfect animal for one where a vow offering demands a flawless one. The last collection of this kind was for the tabernacle, where the people brought so much that Moses had to order them to stop (Exodus 36:5-7).

Verse 4 has David give three thousand talents of gold of Ophir and seven thousand talents of refined silver from his own treasury. A talent is about 75 pounds, so three thousand talents is on the order of 112 tons of gold. These are national treasury numbers, gathered over a forty-year reign of tribute and plunder, not a private purse.

Verse 7 counts ten thousand darics of gold. The daric was a Persian gold coin of about 8.4 grams, roughly a third of an ounce, first struck under Darius I who reigned from 522 to 486 BC, and it was the standard gold piece of the empire that let the exiles come home. It is the unit the Chronicler's own readers used, given here so they could picture the sum.

A source of the finest gold, reached by ship from Ezion-geber on the Gulf of Aqaba, with voyages taking three years round trip (1 Kings 9:26-28, 10:22). Its exact location is not stated in Scripture; the trade route points south along the Arabian or African coast. A potsherd found at Tell Qasile near Tel Aviv is inscribed 'gold of Ophir for Beth-horon, thirty shekels.'

Verse 22 says they made Solomon king 'for a second time.' The first was the emergency ceremony at Gihon during Adonijah's attempt on the throne, where Zadok took the horn of oil from the tent and anointed him with the trumpet sounding (1 Kings 1:38-40). This one is the public assembly with sacrifices, and Zadok is confirmed as priest at the same time.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רֹאֶה (roeh), seer - נָבִיא (navi), prophet - חֹזֶה (hozeh), seer
translationNotes.note: Verse 29 cites three written sources for David's reign, the records of Samuel, Nathan, and Gad, and gives each man a different title. Roeh and hozeh both mean one who sees; navi is the standard word for a prophet who speaks for God. 1 Samuel 9:9 notes the change in usage outright: 'he who is now called a prophet was formerly called a seer.' None of these three books survives.

stories.keyTakeaway: David presents his personal treasures for the temple and calls for contributions; the leaders respond generously with gold, silver, bronze, and iron. David praises God, the people make sacrifices, Solomon is anointed king a second time, and David's reign of forty years concludes.

intro:
1 Chronicles does not name its author. Jewish tradition (preserved in the Talmud, Baba Bathra 15a) attributes the book to Ezra the priest and scribe, who drew on official genealogical records, royal annals, and earlier prophetic histories. The book reached its final form in post-exilic Jerusalem around 450-430 BC, during or shortly after Ezra's reform of the returned community. The same Ezra who later wrote the book of Ezra; the closing verses of 2 Chronicles (36:22-23) are nearly identical to the opening verses of Ezra (1:1-3), which Jewish tradition cites as the textual marker linking the two books as a single literary project from his hand. Tradition also holds that Nehemiah completed the final genealogies of Chronicles after Ezra's death. Ezra was a priest of the line of Aaron through Phinehas (Ezra 7:1-5), a "skilled scribe in the Law of Moses" (Ezra 7:6), sent from Babylon to Jerusalem in 458 BC by the Persian king Artaxerxes I with royal authority to teach the Law and reorganize the temple worship. Jewish tradition holds that Ezra founded the Great Assembly (Knesset Gedolah), the body that helped fix the Hebrew canon and standardize liturgical practice. The events of 1 Chronicles cover from Adam through David's forty-year reign, ending with David's preparations for the temple and Solomon's accession around 970 BC. The historical setting of the writing is the Persian period, with the Achaemenid Empire dominating the ancient Near East and Yehud (the Persian province encompassing former Judah) administered from Jerusalem as a small satrapy. The second temple had been completed in 516 BC under Zerubbabel and the prophetic encouragement of Haggai and Zechariah; the returned community was small, poor, and surrounded by hostile neighbors (Samaritans to the north, Ammonites and Edomites to the south and east). Persia's emperors Cyrus the Great, Darius I, Xerxes I (Ahasuerus of Esther), and Artaxerxes I had each played roles in the restoration. Egypt was a Persian satrapy under the 27th Dynasty; Greece was beginning its Classical period with Athens at its height under Pericles.

1 Chronicles and 2 Chronicles were originally a single Hebrew book called Divrei HaYamim ("Events of the Days" or "Words of the Days"), divided by the Greek Septuagint translators (3rd century BC) into two and renamed Paraleipomena ("Things Omitted"). The Latin Vulgate adopted the Greek division but renamed it Chronica ("Chronicles") at Jerome's suggestion, and English Bibles inherited that title. In the Jewish canon, Chronicles is the closing book of the Ketuvim (Writings) and thus the final book of the Tanakh (Hebrew Bible). Hebrew manuscript fragments of Chronicles were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), with copies dating to the Persian period or shortly after.
